text.p: 1. Durham 1st October 1784

Mr Gill had so much to say about his tour into the west that I could not get from him last night. He has a nephew a son of Joseph, not of Arramathea but Shildon that he wants to put to us, to work and learn farming, we to find him victuals only, Mr Gill clothes, I told him I could say nothing as I had no house, and was rather cold about it, and said he would see you at the fair. But I have been thinking, as he is a smartish boy, writes a good hand and understands accounts he may be useful, however you may think of it, and will see him at the fair, and can talk to Mr Gill about him. May turn him over to me at Whitsuntide, as I suppose Mr Leadbetter will go with you. Pray think William Atkinson on about examining the ewe lambs tails and tups old and young and ewes and gimmals for yellow ones. A young butcher was dressing a sheep in Chester le-Street , and I asked him if they got 4d per lb? Yes replied he smartly for good ones such as yours. I thanked him and rode on. I promised Jack Embleton and Richy Moffat a lot of your Peels sheep when you begin to sell, and I would advise to sell for decent profit at all times, and I am of opinion that mutton will be dear very soon. You will see G. Holmes and Mr Sharp &c at Newcastle fair, join with them to handle a part of Gregsons ewes, when they please at 4d per lb, 21 groats is 7s, 4 times 7 is 28 and 6s offal makes 34s but be content with less money, you know it is very easy to reckon upon paper. It strikes me that you should not sell fat cattle cowardly, why sell fat and buy lean at a fat price. Jack Embleton declared to me that the west country cows were sold at Morpeth on Wednesday at 4/3d per stone. Let James Culley go to Morpeth market some day perhaps he can take it on his road to or from Yarm, and see Redhouse. I give you joy of the good weather. Corn is no worse here and people all leading. Do not neglect to sow the horse close &c when fit, get seed wheat ready and make preparation. I sent a letter by Adam Cummins last night from Newcastle. I have just seen Gilly Starforth and always behold him with fresh astonishment, but everything astonishes about this factory and these people. Old Mr Starforth is still by the seaside but much better. Both Gilly
and George declare they have sent 3 sheets to Morpeth directed for James Crosbe, but no direction where to be left, pray tell Crosbe to enquire for them of all the carriers. Gilly says they are coming north in a week or 2, but it may be I suppose 2 or 3 more weeks first.

Grange. Dined with Mr Robson, young Ralph is a fine boy, Mr Crawford and his son in law fond of him you may be sure. James has 6 stots rising 3. I bid him 7s 6 for 4 they go to Yarm fair on the Monday. If James Culley be for Yarm, he must not attend Wooler, therefore a day or 2 can make no difference, and he may look at these steers. I only name this, do as seems good. Tell Mr Forty I saw his brother and sister all are well. I then went to speak to Mr Dobson, and met with Crosier and George Surtees, Mr Hodgson of Alwent &c &c. George Surtees like drunk at ten o'clock in the morning, Crosier fat, very civil all. But let me return to the honest though greasy butcher, Mr Matt. You know what I am going to say, we get more by these greasy butchers than the fat Surtees's. Mr Dobson says he sells mutton at 4d that good mutton and beef are both scarce and is of opinion that there is a probability of mutton and small beef being scarcer between and Candlemas 2 February new style than in spring because the consumption is so small poor people can't afford to buy, is not this likely reasoning, and may teach you and us to sell for profit all along. He says he does not kill half the large sheep he used to at this season and his neigbours the same. Bought the other day of the Cook &c near 400 small sheep and near 30 cattle. I think you must buy Mr John Robsons wethers, and may enquire about Mr Wilsons of Islington. I now think dear as sheep are they will pay till Christmas, but am not fond of keeping all till spring, your own dinmonds &c must be kept.

Barmton. Mr Collings prize tup is not very capital to handle, but rather catchy to look at. It looks like Mr Wastles judgement weakening Mr Collings says he has let one to George Lax &c better than him but not so pleasing to look at, he was gone so did not see him, let at 9 guineas also, Mr Colling will not be a mar trade. He is clear for letting at good prices or none. Mr Colling has some promising lambs, which I am glad off. Wheat a better crop here than I expected, oats a bad one, beans good and barley good, this last grain I am inclined to think has a chance to get a fall people have got that idea upon their tongues end, therefore perhaps
you had better sell a part. So much cider and the crop universally good in England.

Yarm 2 October. Found my cousins as well as could be expected and my sister and Nelly well thank God. Tell James and my sister at Eastfield I pray that she must not come to the fair as room is not to be had, upon which account my sister and Nelly set of for the north next week, that they may not crowd them at the fair. I need not remind you of paying attention to Matt. Make my best respects and wishes to my sister and James, accept same yourself and believe me at all times ire truly offed
Goo Culley

PS As my sister has seen me, she and her niece propose setting forward in the beginning of next week, but as they may stop a day or 2 at Newcastle, you are not to expect them until they come. I was at Burton, Mr Wastle poorly, Mrs Wastle very well. Mr Wastle says beef must be 2s 8d before March. Northallerton a pretty good show of cattle, and not quite so high as have been. I send this by your friend Mr John Mason to Alnwick fair. Bob got here with the tups all well by 6 o'clock but I have not seen them. Mr Wastle says Mr Charge sent bad quays into Russia. Tell Nanny Brown I saw her brother Jack, who desired his love, and his wife is still poorly.
2. Northallerton 6th October 1784
Dear Matty

I left Barmton this morning Mr Colling in company, saw 6 very good 4 years old oxen of John Laxes, and at Smeeton saw a famous cow bought of James Brown Oldborough at 26£ out of pocket. They are bought by a steward of Sir George Stricklands and its supposed for a gentleman near Bristol who married Sir George's daughter, several more bought but not arrived. The tups were gone when I got here. Nothing but single horse carts here, most drive 2 and many 3. I passed 9 drove by a man and 2 boys, I asked how they did upon passing waggons &c. He says 'Wayey if we turn yan o them out od way they all follow' but I must observe Mr Matt that these are broad and good smooth roads. However they will soon come up to the Irish. I have met with some gentlemen receiving taxes who advised me to write to you to enter a horse form and say that if I ride 90 horses I need only pay for one, but Matthew Galloway must pay they say, that is, every person must pay for But if William Brown &c rides upon a young horse on breaking, or making up for sail &c he is not taxable.

7th October Birdforth. We are to have 2 stots of Richmond 13£ very little I shall get Richmond to send them to Mr Collings (Barmton) before Yarm fair, so James may take them up, and I will get Mr Colling to pay him for them. His tup pleasing but not very fat, an admiral. Billy Walker sold most of Mr James Ewes at Allerton at 21s 6 per . I have a notion they would do him good, but I wont say they that bought them will profit much. Firkins 33s the highest for dairies. Weather keeps very good and mild. Mr Brough has arrived. James should pay him for the 2 steers at Yarm, and he will allow for the tup 2£ 2 only, as he had only 18 lambs got by him.

Saturday 9th Milton. I am determined to show the large tup on Monday though I believe I shall meet with some rubbers. Mr Sails tups are come, also Clevers &c skin still their object. Coaching horses I am told are scarce and were sold at Howden though others could not, it appears to me absurd in our way to breed any other than strong horses. Wheat good in this market sold for 6 to 7s per bushel oats 18d per quarter, barley 27, turnips pretty good and bought from 2£ to 2 15 per acre. Mutton 4d to 4 1/2, beef 4d. Mr Cleaver has insisted upon having 10 ewes tupped of J. Taylor by big tup. I am to dine with him tomorrow. I saw him and he is bright, pleased with the tup, and like a man acknowledges ours are the best sheep in England save Dishley. Mr Cleaver behaves like a gentleman and was always candid. I saw the tups and indeed they are strange ones, shin with a witness and no more I beg pardon heads and bones. Farewell in haste
Goo Culley
3. Sawton 10th October 1784
Dear Matty

I sent you a letter from Milton yesterday. Afterwards we took a look at the tups which were comed to the fair against Monday, my friend B. Sails make only a middling figure. He was not come himself. A Mr Lees of Lackenby much worse, this young man has been thorough Lincolnshire and hired a tup of Mr Chapling a rare skinned one he says, such a one as will please the Wolds people. Surpassing strange! These people do not see thorough their delusion, no wonder my brother James lost his useful sheep by breeding to the tastes of these mistaken folks. I am very sure you cannot conceive how bad these sheep are. I would not have missed coming this road upon any account, when they will awaken from their delirium I know not. I asked young Lee if the tup he had hired of Mr Chaplin was fat, he candidly confessed he was not, but a deal of bone, and skin thats
the thing Mr Matt. The fattest sheep he saw were at Mr Codds of Bakewells kind, but said they were little waddling toads . Everybody are running upon big ones, I assure you Mr Matt therefore if you want to pursue the tup trade, you must have some large ones. I have made a mistake in sending the little tup here, they say hes only fit for a fallow field. What a charming country this is? How hospitable the farmers? No wonder the poor Scots never wish to return from it. You must not wonder if I stay among them, they are so fond of me. We like far too well.

11th October Monday. A good show of oxen and very high sold from 22 to 28£ a pair. Straw oxen they call them but fit for turnips. A strange show of tups. Mr Sail let 11 out of 12 and not one good one, but they were next best to ours, which was looked on with astonishment, indeed he made a famous figure amongst these thick skiels and skins, we had much credit, and it is not impossible but we may have some visitors from this quarter. Our tup was so much handled that I was afraid it might hurt him. Mr Taylor talks of keeping him another year, but will write to us. One of the (John) Wreinghams sent his compliments to James and talks of being over between and Candlemass. I could have let a few tups tolerably well I think, though they are not fond of going above 5 guineas. Mr Sail let some at no more than 3 and Messrs C ? Cleaver and Kendal from 1/2 to 3 guineas, sold many very low I dare say, it is amazing to me that they do not try to get better, because they confess they are wrong, and many of the Wolds people are or seem to be convinced of their mistake, and they must necessarily change the sort. I am of opinion they are ashamed to come to us, because they were in our country, though Mr Cleaver is to have 10 ewes tupped by our tup and he candidly owns, and has said to many people, John Taylor one, that ours were best in England except Mr Bakewells and he thought ours as good. We went from Milton past Howden and crossed the Ouse a Dutch river or done into Marsland as they call it equal I suppose to the banks of Nile and where they improve land worth almost nothing to near a £ an acre, by letting on the tides and warping it they can cover it with this warp or sleech and mud in very little time to one or even 2 foot thick but the thicker the longer of drying and being fit for tillage, it then brings most plentiful crops of grain &c in short the improvement is beyond conception. All this country is a moss below, and thousands of trees are dug up wherever they make their cuts &c or dig peats, in the moors which are an amazing tract of land laying behind the good land, which good land has been indisputably made by these rivers before the drainage took place. Lord Percy has a fine estate here and highly improvable. This mode of improvement had been used some time
ago but laid aside and now renewed with fresh vigour and not likely to be lost until all be lost as my friend Ben Sail says. We were at a Mr Empsons looking at some large oxen but not capital old and corking about a hundred. Mr Sail has a desire for your quays and best oxen, but is not determined to go over yet, if he goes for Carlisle he will probably take road by Fenton.

Thursday morning 14th October . We arrived here yesterday. Old Rumps very fresh and clever, I think indeed full as young as last year, this is very good to like and very fat, he has worn better than any of his brothers I know of and has been hard used. I own I am pleased with him. 2 tolerable ewes comed with him to be tupped. I met here with your letter of the 3rd inst for which I thank you most heartily, hearing from ones friends is to me like a drink to the thirsty or rest to the weary. I am happy to hear all are well, my best wishes attend you all and beg my compliments to your two female guests. I forgot to tell you Mr Bates joined me at Milton in the fair morning and is very well. Mr Colling did not come though he promised but I had a letter from him to this place along with yours to enquire about Milton tup show &c. He bids fair to drive out Mr Sail &c from that market if he chooses for I think every requisite is cantered in Mr Colling necessary to form a capital tup breeder. I hope sister and Nelly are arrived and I flatter myself your corn is mostly in by this, if your weather has been equal to ours. Be not afraid of your old wheat, new wheat its true is better all the way as I go south but like last year its all or mostly ill fed, not perfected, and all corn seems as though it would not be low. Barley 28 to 30s here I think oats are as dear with you as anywhere I have been. I am glad Mr Wilson takes the Old Thing the price of his 3 are 30 guineas then if I remember right. It's a great price for Mr Gregsons ewes 25s per but to be kept until March is a long while and if good perhaps should Mr Edison came from Wakefield here last night says not so good quite as it was but good enough, and expects an advance by Christmas or sooner. But one thing frightens me respecting mutton, viz. the immense quantities off fruit everywhere, it is utterly impossible for you to form any idea of the quantities 200 waggon and cart loads are said to go every week to Leeds market of apples &c. You may rest assured we have rare times amongst them, consequently poor people will and do live much upon apple pies &c and very lucky it is for the butchers all say mutton would not have been met with if the demand had been as usual. Still I think mutton must be 4d and I would
advise to sell always for profit. We shall leave this place in 2 or 3 days. I hope to meet with letters at Dishley. My horse stands his journey well but continues to sweat immoderately. Have you heard from Richard? Or did you not see him at Alnwick. Has Bill Pickering hired a tup? Has G. Logan never seen the dinmonds yet? Let me know all about Wooler fair? Excuse this scrawl and believe me yours always
Goo Culley
I am glad Matt behaves well, tell him his father often thinks of him and will love him if he is a good boy. Did you buy Joe's steers?

Monday morning. Dear Sisters. I send you Goose last letter. Be so good as return yours in 2 or 3 days. Shall be glad to see Nelly over to day as the ladies go away tomorrow. Shall be glad to hear of little Nelly being better. Everyone sends best respects with ire offed brother Matt Culley
4. Wentbridge 15th October (Friday) 1784
Dear Matty

I sent you a letter yesterday and propose going south tomorrow. I think if G. Logan has not sold those lambs of the Lord of Hilton you should buy them. Lambs were sold from 14 to 16 per at Darlington, large but bad, and at 12 to 14 upon the Wolds. Mr Sail goes on briskly in the tup trade, let 11 at Milton and 2 since we came home. I think we stand a chance for his custom afterwards, he talks of looking at the dinmond tup at Mr Collings. I would gladly have him to come your way to Carlisle to look at our cattle for winterers, but I am afraid he will not. I have told him of Mr Thompsons 2 heifers and the best ox (Walkers) also Purvis's steer and he would probably pick out 2 or 3 from Mrs Comptons oxen. Its possible he may come, but would have me write to you to send up the 4 I first mentioned, but I said I would not as I would gladly have him go, so he says he will write to you himself. He wants 7 head of cattle, so I said we had 8 clever bullocks bought of Mrs Compton, from which he might pick 2, 3 or 4, but he still replies he cannot go, and that you know better than he what he wants, so whether he comes or not I know not. If he does not pray do to the best of your knowledge, and you can meet with the cattle upon the road and he and I can settle the price please God as I return. If he should come show him your tups, what you use, and the dinmonds as well as you can, but show Blewcap &c and some of the best dinmonds by themselves at last. If you send him the cattle unseen give me your opinion of the weights and what you think they should be by stone before they come away. And on second thoughts had you not
better send one of your own drivers all the way for fear of worst by being ill drove? (suppose Lisle Johnson William Atkinsons best man.) Sheep continue very high in all markets fat and lean. Mutton everywhere 4d per lb but that high price I think is much against the consumption.

Friday afternoon. This moment Mr Sail received 2 letters one from Arnold with Mr Bakewells compliments to Mr Sail and self, that Mr Bakewell was gone to Caistor fair but will be glad to see us after Monday. The other from Mr Bakewell himself, wishing to see Mr Sail and me after Monday as he was on his road to Caistor. If it had come in the morning I believe we should all have gone to Caistor to have met this old gentleman amongst the Lincolnshire geniuses, but only observe how he concludes 'I will only say that as brother Chips Mr Sail and Mr Culley will not have any objection to being informed the tup season is likely to finish well, for since Monday the 4th some have been let at 20, some at 30, 1 at 40 and one at 100 guineas'. Yrs &c R. Bakewell. Mr Popplewell offered to buy me a boar and sow of the right Berkshire kind but we have not fixed how to get them to Fenton yet. Mr Sail thinks it best to have a cart for one horse made here to take home scythes sickles &c and can load her out with nails &c would one put the pigs in? Sow is to be with pigs.

Rotheram Monday 18th October . Mr Sail came with us to this place last night. This the week market, the fortnight days are best which as the same week as Wakefield, then what remains unsold goes forward to Wakefield this market is held upon a very dry clever piece of ground with oblong square pens for sheep like Morpeth only these are fixed, as well as those for cattle. Which last are high raised as you may suppose and very convenient indeed the pens for the cattle are open at one end. Cattle sold rather below 4s mostly long horns or half breed, and consequently steerish and not very fat, sheep 4 1/2 sink very indifferent ones in general, except one lot with light skins, totally different from all the rest which were in general from Lincolnshire, but the few I mention I traced to Meadow place poor Mr Algoods I mean, the tup that got them came from that neighbourhood, no good ones Mr Matty but what may be traced to Dishley. Mr Sails sheep are at turnips near this town, and a middling lot only I think, will take some making fat.

Mansfield 22 miles from Rotherham. We have just dined here upon good beef stake, and intend for Redhills tonight. Barley 32 per quarter, amazing quantities of malt made here, our landlord says 30000 quarters is carried by land to Chesterfield, Buxton and even Manchester. 3000 people employed in making common white thread and hosiery. We parted with honest Ben and his agreeable nonsense at Rotheram. I still think he will see you in his road from Carlisle though he says not. I have given him
orders for 6 doz. scythes and 30 doz. sickles and to load out with nails of different sizes. Suppose you were to order some table knives and forks &c or anything else that can be had from that quarter, that my sisters or you and James may think of, in the spring will be soon enough for the cart to go down, but Ben will write if he does not come and then you and William Brown &c can order what scythes and sickles &c &c &c you please. Redhill evening. We here met with one of the great Sponsors London horse dealers, who had come with Charles Hodgkinson from Harborough fair. This Spencer furnishes with horses 3 of the regiments of light horse. I bid Charles tell you that we were so far well. He will probably see you at Newcastle fair for which place he sets of in a few days. Charles said good horses will be dear at Newcastle though Spencer says the tax will hurt. I find this horse fair goes badly down, and people are at a loss what to enter.

Dishley Tuesday 19 October . Disappointed at not receiving a letter from you. Mr Bakewell not come home, and if he does not come to night, shall go to Mr Stubbins's tomorrow. We have had a walk thorough Dishley stock, in part with honest Breedon, the best tups all gone, but what are left exceed what ever we have seen, farther than ever. Such ewes as strike me with fresh wonder, he leads and ever will as long as he lives. I find the tup Mr Bakewell has let the other day for 100 guineas is the other brother to him that was let at 80 to near Spilsby and 20 ewes served, what do you think of your shearings now Mr Matt, they are brothers. You may tell Mr Logan this is the sheep Mr Bakewell wrote to him about after his return home and offered at 60 guineas. Mr Bakewell is just come so must give over at present and finish in the morning. Mr and Mrs Bakewell desire compliments, Miss Smith desires hers to Matt and Nelly.

Wednesday morning. Just 3 weeks since I left you and no letters by this mornings post so shall finish this and send you, for your not writing is no excuse to me. Mr Bakewell says Mr North is to be here on Thursday to wait on your humble servant you see what respect I have found in this enlightened country Mr Matt. Enough to swell a man of less vanity than that of brother George. Mr Thomas Bates and I go for Mr Stubbins today, and return to Loughborough market tomorrow and where then I know not. Mr Bakewell talks of going to a fair at Horncastle ever we attend, and may be out some days, but I may do Dishley, as I can think of no other place at present and sh easy if I do not hear now and then from you. Mr Bakewell says as the entering of one horse apiece sufficient, supposes the Act can mean no more, and that you have no occasion to pay for your servant riding about among the work people. Mr Bakewell
seems to have the ball at his foot now, and you may be sure he will play it to advantage, he refused 50 guineas for the tupping of 20 ewes from a Mr Green in Lincolnshire the other day, same as had Rumps, and thinks Mr Green would give 100 for 40, which Mr Bakewell calls only half a rode, what will the matter come to think you? He says there will be some sport another year, those that live to see it. The matter is not to overdo it, but they have drove of several customers, and Mr Breedon has catched them, but not made the most of them Mr Bakewell thinks. Its lucky for us 2 hand folks that they do them so high here, we must live under their feet at any rate and be thankful, but one thing is clear to me, always to do a few well rather than many badly. I am with very sincere regard to everybody ire ever aff
Goo Culley
PS Perhaps you will not be plagued with such long letters in future as we shall now be much engaged with Mr Bakewell.
5. Dishley 24th October 1784 (Sunday)
Dear Matty

I have this morning received your long, kind, and friendly letter, for which I beg you will accept my best thanks. I was very anxious to hear from you indeed! All this kind family, with my worthy companion join me in respectful compliments. The weather has been most favourable indeed, seems now to be changing, as we have had a coarse night last night and a little snow fallen though no quantity of wet yet, the ground is so dry in this quarter that people cannot sow wheat. You have done very well in the tup letting way, I am vastly pleased with what you have done only I think if Mr G. Logan would give 30 guineas for the 3 dinmonds it might do very well, but I would not abate one shilling of that. Mr Gregsons ewes may do, keeping considered, though it is a very high price. I hope Mr Robsons ewes and wedders are better bought. I am glad you have sent a part to Mr Sharps turnips and recommend to take a fair profit at any time. These ladies have made a short stay with my sister. Bill Gill is the properest man I know of to buy or hire a good horse. Am glad your corn markets keep so good, and I think it right to be doing in part though most people think that corn will be well sold, yet they expect barley to lower a little. You do not mean that Bartholomew Brown sells oats at 18s per 6 bushels? If so it is the highest price I have heard of. I am glad that you have dealt with Mr William Bates. A Mr Gibson who manages the brewery near Hexham has a brother at or near Lichfield who has bought 20 ewes of Mr Paget
for his brother in the north at 3 guineas per and a tup at Mr Pagets are good sheep, very different from anything they have had I dare say, what can these people mean by going so deep. Am happy your tups keep improving pray pay attention to them and the tup lambs, if you are not 2d you are far forward. By Mr Bakewells own confession, we are 3d in his alphabet, viz we have been longest in the Dishley blood except Mr Stubbins. I am glad Crosbe has sold so many cattle, it will help to pay your debts for you must owe a deal. I hope Mr Bates is right in the tup Mr Embleton should have had. I suppose Tommy Embletons ewes cheap. I hope Mr Sail has been with you ere now and bought your best cattle? I care not how few you winter, you can pay the more attention to sheep and tups &c. You did well to quit your bad dinmonds, did you not sell the bad gimmals? Sheep must have been high at Wooler fair and are so everywhere if a check do not come before spring. Have you sown the horse close? We have been at Mr Stubbins and saw Cambrels the 100 guineas tup, a good tup but not good enough everywhere at the price, but he can let at his own price now Mr Breedon and Bettison have him between them. Mr Bakewell has refused 50 guineas for tupping 20 ewes since by a tup Mr Princeps used last season, he has faults too, but the people here are all infected with that kind of enthusiasm which perhaps its lucky we were inocculated with long ago. Poor Mr Walkers aged father has had a stroke of the palsy and lies dangerously ill, so we are not likely to see his son suddenly. We have had Deverel, Buckley, and many other geniuses, indeed they pay me too much respect. We were to have gone to Horncastle fair but are now for Burton, but may change again, the old boy has much to do and often changes, Mr Smith of Birmingham and a son and daughter here, also a young Russian, a fine boy, has been here near a year. One of the Wildboars stays here constantly too. Mr Bakewells cabbages planted in April very good, and those in the latter end of May very well. Carrots thick but not long, owing perhaps to the carrots being prevented from getting lower for the sods that are first turned down before the soil is ploughed upon them, what you call double spitting. I find the rape stood the last winter well, and they prefer it to stubble turnips or anything else. Breedon says they would scarce get better of it in April and May. Mr Buckley says the same. Mr Bakewell is very fond of saving land in winter, I mean pasturage, what ever he can. Pray keep Matt with you if not inconvenient to my sister (your wife) but if he disturbs her let him go. Be sure you examine your ewe lambs for yellowness, and all your tups and tup lambs, there can be no harm in it and it is of much importance for us to be clear of every malady we can, it will hurt Will Marshall much
I think. Mr Thompson had wrote to Mr Bakewell for his last years tup at 20 guineas but Mr Bakewell let him at home for 30, I think we have a much better chance from Mr Bakewell letting at such extravagant prices, none but tupmen can come to Dishley, none else can afford it, and we can do very well with less prices. Mr Bakewell let a tup to Mr Buckley at 40 and bid him 20 guineas to be of, and had a customer at 80, but Buckley would not. A nice sheep with wool or pelt and extreme small bones, it is unaccountable what prices they have got to. Mr Bakewell says there will be sport next season they that live to see it. Mr Logan will probably come, but if he be for a good one will be high taxed, therefore think he is wrong in putting of a year, besides 100 is too much for him to give in his present situation, but he must judge for himself. A capital one will not be had at Dishley another year under 100. You may put down Mr John Taylors 2 tups at 21£. I suppose Cheviot will be well covered as the Forest hills are white this morning. The Revd Sir Horace Trelawny from ditto in Cornwall bought 4 heifers of Mr Bakewell last Thursday but I have not learned price. Mr Bakewell talks of our going to see him but perhaps we shall not as the season is cooled.

Monday 25 October (Burton upon Trent). We are just got here to a fair, horses very high, 2 year old colts 25£ per many of them. Mr Walker of Woolsthorpe came to Dishley last night. His father has had a stroke of the palsy lately but is better though not out of danger. We are to visit Mr Walker after this jaunt. Mr Walker says the London market has been very bad for fat lately, and from present appearances there seems to be a dammback at present in many parts of the south, this may be from turnips failing &c but I am of an opinion it would not effect you, as such numbers of goods have come south. I do not find that any sheep have let for above 30 guineas Dishley excepted, and not many at that, this is obvious from Dishley being the fountain head of the fashionable stock.

Lichfield 28th October . Laid here all night and had Mr Gibson a linen draper, whose brother manages for the company of the Hexham brewery, he has bought more than 50 ewes, from different people, 20 from Mr Paget at 3 guineas and 1/2 guinea for tupping, these are to be feared Mr Matt but he has luckily bought a few gimmals and a tup of Jack Raby, and which tup I hope they will be so kind as cross Mr Pagets ewes with afterwards and that will I think do their job. You need not take any notice of this Sir, but I would have been as pleased if they had kept from Mr Paget or the Dishley tribe. We had also your friend Whitfield, very civil poor man but I am afraid does not fall into much business and is not very popular. Mutton 4 1/2 here. But at Tamworth fair last Monday sheep
were heavily sold and were said to drop 1/2 per lb, however they were all sold, some say 10000 sheep (fat) some shearings sold at 32s per, is not very low, but turnips being a bad crop in general and the consumption of butchers meat less on account of its high price and plenty of apples, may make this flatness upon fat stock, but most people think, fat must be high. The London markets have been very bad some weeks from same cause perhaps. Corn markets much the same all the way from the middle of Yorkshire viz. wheat 6 to 6/4 barley 3/6 to 3/9 but everybody think the latter must drop from the very great crop. Oatmeal advances in the west and that grain is said to yield badly.

29th October Birmingham. Dined here and once more beheld this busy place with fresh pleasure, went to Hornby a small town with a fair for cattle, horses, hops and onions. Hops 5£ per cwt. Cattle rather flat. Stratford upon Avon stands in a fine country then to Shipstone in Worcestershire wheat 36 quarter worth 8s, barley 30s. Next day 30th to Mr Fowlers, where we saw the best horned cattle I ever saw, but descended from Dishley. Mr Fowler a steady sensible Quaker has a tup from Mr Bakewell at 40 which he has hired again at 60, and only a clumsy sheep in my opinion. Mr Fowler went with me to Mrs Rayns (J. Surtees). She cried for joy. 31st to Warrick, where we saw 3 capital long horned oxen of Lord Warricks. November 1st Coventry fair. Fat cattle better sold and sheep sharp, but London market is got up again, was exceedingly bad. 2d. Shelton Mr Huskisson in good spirits, and Jack. Miss at Ashby with her sister who is under Dr Thicklands care and in a poor way by accounts. Mr Huskisson has bought me a filly and a colt which we shall take down in our hands if we get no more, but if we buy any more shall write to you to send a man up, as it is very uncertain when we shall return if all keep well want some money and not very little if we buy 1/2 a dozen horses and stay long, but will let you know more of that in another letter. These good people will part with cash at present. Still amazing dry weather, sometimes a little hazy but no wind.

Dishley Wednesday 3rd November . Just returned from our 10 days tour, where I received 2 letters from you and one from Mr Sail. I am sorry for Mr Sail but mistakes will happen, I never promised Mr Wastle, I only said they would have made good ones in his hands, but he's a deep one and can turn anything to his own liking. Pray tell me if you think I should take any more from him on my return. I spoke to Mr Stubbins about wood and he is to make enquiry. I am a little surprised about B. Tulip and Bill Hunter, but wonders never cease. Mr Brown's failure shows how cautious people should be in trusting people with mortgages &c. You
must continue writing to Dishley though we may be often from home, and you may depend upon hearing from me from every quarter of the kingdom be where I will. About the 15th we talk of going south either to Mr Youngs or to return by him, undetermined yet. If we go a long journey I fancy we shall both have to borrow, as money goes apace I assure you. Mr Thomas joins in good wishes with ire offed
Goo Culley
6. Dishley 4th November 1784
Dear Matty

On our arrival here last night I finished a long letter and sent you, in answer to 3 I have had since I wrote, for which accept my best thanks. I met with the 2 last both last night, one begun the 22nd the other 25th ult . I am extremely obliged to you for my attention to my child, the Almighty will reward you and my sister for it, I cannot do it equal to my wishes. If you could see Mr of Belford any time, I would wish him to go to school another summer certainly. I hope my sister keeps pretty well as you say nothing in your two last, may she have a happy moment and all go well. Mr Bakewell talks of going into the west and my friend Thomas is afraid of the expense and talks of returning soon. I should be glad of his company but would be sorry to lead him into unnecessary expenses. Indeed money goes like dike water, but my brother my kind brother never said I spent too much, but if you wish us not to go I will return with Mr T. Bates whenever you please, it is my duty and was always a pleasure to me to return to such kind friends and I hope ever will. Be sure you tell William Brown that I often think of him, and all our connections. Upon my word T. Tulip is a manager if he has brought about a union with his sister and Scot. I do not understand that story of my aunt Hunters, it is unpleasant. I am glad Ralph Reid &c is alive. I am glad that so many sheep and cattle have come south from you, if turnips are cheap do not finish your own stock of all kinds, Mr Bakewell is clear for eating turnips, cabbages, and carrots &c early, his reasons are they never do stock so much good as in the autumn, nor never go so far, stock as it were become naturalised to them before the bad weather comes on, and if they eat turnips &c they save the grass, which keeps always better than turnips, and the more grass you save until spring the better, and the first saved is
always best, and he is more an advocate than ever for leading turnips off, says if Mr Collingwood was properly talked to, he would allow leading of, as the taking from. A must improve B in proportion, and it cannot be supposed you want to take them on to another persons premises, besides the truer turnips are eat the more passes thorough the animal machine, consequently the more valuable manure which is the case when led off, but when eaten many tops shells &c are wasted which cant do the same good as when it passes through the animal, but I am afraid John Trumble and Master are too narrow to properly consider these philosophic principles. I do not recollect that we were to take Mr William Walker of Beals stock. I am glad you have got your stock all to turnips, the weather is so favourable they must do well, and by all means I would recommend to sell for a reasonable profit, you can always either buy more or keep your store stock better which is highly important. My father Atkinson is elderly and I am afraid does not always live so regularly as he ought. Its pleasing to hear that the daughters and grandchildren of fat Crops are so pleasing, if you can properly mix or blend the valuable qualities of fat Crops and Blewcap you will almost rival Dishley, for I confess though we are nearly equal (situation and keeping considered) to most of his neighbours yet we are a good deal short of Mr Bakewell still, but be thankful that you are in his best blood, and let us make the most of it. What Dishley will come to I know not, nor what they have made this season I know not for they decline speaking, but I have a notion more than 1000 of tups a good deal and I shall not be surprised if he makes 500 of 5 sheep next season for you see they have made 100 each of 2 this year, and have had 60 bred by Mr Codd for 1/2 the rode of his tup for next season, he pays 60 for his whole use this year, and I was by when Mr Bakewell let Mr Fowler a middling sheep for 60 next year for which he pays 40 this, that whatever Mr Logan does, we and many people will be shut out and I think my friend George will be gravelled a little, if they come to ask him 100 or 120 for his favourite next season and I rather think that may be the case. Sir William Erskine is very genteel and I approve of your answer to him. I am sorry you sold no horses at Newcastle, the mare you bought must I think be cheap perhaps I am doing wrong in procuring young horses in this country. I dare say James has bought these heifers cheap of Mr Purvis. Many people are unable to sow wheat in the vale and in all the clay country, it is so dry a time for the snow only fell upon the high country and to the westward. Mr Walker of Woolsthorpes father died yesterday week. I find Mr John Bates (who I am sorry to say was robbed poor man) and I were wrong in not buying all the Hilton sheep you had offered, but
I think times have held out better with you than in the south for in parts here the store sheep have dropped a little. By a letter from Mr Sail last night he scolds me, but expresses his satisfaction at your anxiety and wish to serve him. I have told him in my answer today that it was his own fault in writing to Denton and asking so many foolish questions, were we going to send him or recommend any cattle to him but what were nice ones, he should have gone to Fenton. What way have you commissioned your oil cakes? They are not to be had in this country under 6£ or 7£ per ton, they say they can sell them for 6£ per ton ground down for manure. You are right beef cannot drop this winter now especially as London market is up again though Mr Sail says Wakefield was very bad on Wednesday, but that must have been owing to the Lincolnshire men sending too much stock to Wakefield in consequence of the London markets being so bad but I hope that will change again soon. It matters not if Mr Browns business was 2000 per annum if he did not look after his affairs, the larger the concern always the more danger Mr Matt, therefore it behoves us to be vigilant attentive circumspect &c. You remember Mr Peas at Darlington, and I blame Mr G. Logan and everyone that meddles with so many different kinds of business. I have always thought it best to pursue that line that we have been most conversant with. I am glad you have been able to pay your credit, keep that up if you borrow of a bank. I am sorry to ask you Mr Matt: at this dead time for money but as we have bought 2 young horses at 20£ and may buy more and half our cash is already near expended, I believe if you can make it convenient, you must be so kind as get our friend Capt. Ralph Forster of Berwick to give you a bill upon London at 30 or 40 days (if your pinched Mr Forster will give you a little time for the money) for 50£. You must observe to enclose the bill in a cover directed to Mr Bakewell Loughborough, then if Mr Bakewell and I happen to be from Dishley, Arnold will open it, and give you immediate advice of the receiving of it. You may at same time write to me another letter which will when I come to Dishley again acquaint me with the bill or it is possible the bill and your letter may reach this place before we go south as our departure is very uncertain, and you will be sure to do this job as soon as you conveniently can. I asked Mr Bakewell if a draft upon Surtees and Burton would do and he says it could not be negotiated here or else I have stamps but I should have got leave of that bank to have drawn on their bankers London. I am in haste yours affectly
Goo Culley

Loughborough one of the clock. I have been thinking if 50£ is too much for you to spare send me a 40£ bill. Is it not amazing that this extraordinary genius should be able to electrify so many people with the same or nearly the same degree of enthusiasm, and as it were to draw them all to one focus or point, for in fact he has convinced the unbelievers of the truth of his sheepish doctrine. I was shown some letters from Lincolnshire where they candidly confess their errors and mistaken opinions, and as that is the case, what may he not be able to accomplish, for Lincolnshire is a large field that has got more to do than any other country almost that I am acquainted with and Warrickshire from being so near akin to Lincoln has got a good deal also to do, that it would seem now as though he would have a chance to do a deal at strange unheard of prices.
7. Dishley 10th November 1784
Dear Brother

I hope you have not forgot to gather a quantity of haws to raise quicks? I sent you 2 letters near together and in the last requested a 40 or 50£ bill. We have been at Mr Pagets and have seen the ewes bought for Mr Donkin, they are no better than I expected, not very good handlers, though I am certain better than any they have ever had, and tupped by a pretty good sheep. Which sheep Mr Paget has made 40 guineas of this season, besides what ewes he has served of his own. Mr Paget is very clever, has got well forward, but is far short of Dishley. We are now going to visit Mr Walker of Woolsthorpe, and to be back at Loughborough fair on Saturday. Mr Jones of Horton is to go with us. My friend T. Bates was talking of leaving me, but is now determined to stay as long as I stay, from an indulgent letter received today from his honest brother. We have been down at Mr Walkers, who I still think is a clever youth, his sheep pretty good, the vale is a fine country, Belvoir a small castle but wonderful situation, and prospect truly astonishing. My honest friend Mr Jones went with us, we came back to Loughborough fair, which was dear for cattle and horses also foals. We went to Dishley all night where we had Mr Walker who came home with us, Mr Paget, Mr Knowles, &c &c, a rare deal of talk upon tups, bulls, &c &c. Next day Sunday went and dined with Mr Jones and next morning Mr Walton brought me your last letter dated 8 of October instead of November I fancy, but notwithstanding that mistake Mr Matt I was happy to receive it, pleasing intelligence to hear of you all keeping well, and of my children behaving well, may you all keep well and their behaviour continue, I pray God and may we return
to you in health and safety. Wheat rather drops in these markets, but everybody are of opinion that it will be dear in future as wheat yields badly in general, barley rises now 28 to 30s and people begin to think it will stand price though a very large crop. Oats 16 to 18s and likely to hold price. Many say that wheat must be dear another year as little has been yet sown in these midland counties, owing to the very dry time which has continued until yesterday when we had a wet day, but this 16th day of November is a very fine morning. We are now at Holme, the Stubbins all well and desire along with Mr Walker their best respcts. Mr Watt has neglected to enquire about wood, but on enquiring of a carpenter of Grantham who Mr Walker employs he says he cannot sell spikes under 4s per gang, 25 to the gang sets felloes 9s per dozen, axle trees 3 shafts per pair 3s 6.

16 November . We are much obliged to you Sir, for your kindness in promising to remit us some money 40£ will do very well I believe as I shall now buy no more horses, and perhaps have done wrong in buying these, though they promise to be useful but I confess high priced 20£ for 2 yearlings besides &cs. It is a little surprising that horses should be so exceeding dear in this country and cheap at Newcastle but they are different kinds of horses, and I know of no horses which pay so much for their keeping and breeding as the blacks, and they are of a much worse kind than they were I think, that valuable kind from Blaze is quite lost and will not be readily recovered, though everyone now almost are growing fond of good middles, light ends, and less bones than they were, the hairy fleshy legs, large buttocks, &c &c are going out of fashion, and well they may, for I still think them most useless animals. I am glad you are going to quit a part of those ewes I bought, I think it always right to sell for a fair profit and to good hands especially, 31s 6d is a great price, but I suppose Crosbe has given Mr Singleton a choice. Pray how do you stand with him? I am always and shall be I think cautious after T. Matthews, for I look upon that money as mostly lost, and Lowry though he has given famous prices and good profits for those cows, should be kept short in hand, as well as our friend Richmond. There can be no crime in attending honestly to ones interests and too much credit often injures both seller and buyer. I am very glad that James Crosbe has sold the 4 cows he bought of Buckley for so much profit. As to Starforth he has and ever will be an inconsistent being, but if his money is safe I can forgive the rest though very unpleasant, however you are right to write to him in severe terms he can bear it all, and money he must pay against your rent. I am afraid Mr Anderson will not take bills upon him, though Surtees and Burton would negotiate them and you can draw them at a short date. I am glad your markets keep so good. Beef is scarce 4s here except nice, mutton indeed holds 4d per lb. tallow same as with you and shins 3 s to 3s 6d per which
I suppose exceeds Newcastle &c. I know Mr Sail blames me, but the blame rests with himself in part, but mostly with Mr Wastle. Mr Wastle is a surprising man to be a dying, however the price pays you very well. I will remember to give Mr Sail 10s 6d I think. I am very surprised how you come to think that oxen would not drive to Mr Sails? Well you have made an excellent end of the sheep you have sold hitherto which shows you can do as well without me as with me. You do well to to let me know that you have sown so much wheat, think you not that I am interested in all you do? How surprisingly late you harvest, I mean the ruff close &c and Mr Thompson is compared with everything here? I advise to sow all the wheat you can with propriety, many people tire of sowing wheat in this country, because it runs the land wild after oats &c, but that is a reason why you should sow more. You rejoice me with saying your turnips are so good, God be thanked. They are very indifferent here in general but they sow with dung in common. You have worked up T. Clark and R. Mills to better prices than I could have expected at so late season. Mr Bakewell lets as low as 4 guineas to neighbours who are no tupmen. I think I shall not quarrel with Mr Wastell, but I shall certainly talk a little to him. Mr Sail should have come to Fenton. Pray tell Mr Leadbetter that I am highly obliged to him for his behaviour to my son, and pray tell Matt that his father will love him for being a good lad. Do you ever examine his pockets? I hope my sister and you are sensible of my gratitude for your kindness to my poor boy, I pray God reward you all. I include all my friends and do not think a weakness to acknowledge that my heart feels when I am upon this subject. I am glad to know that Dr Kerr is to be his master. I have no fear of the doctor making a bad use of it. Be sure you remember me to all my friends and acquaintances. I am really sorry at Mr Pickering's behaviour, it is ill usage to both us and his son William and I think you had better not be too severe until you can see him or see Billy Pickering, as I think Bill has a good deal of honour and honesty. Your brother Bates is gone with Mr Walker to Woolsthorpe this morning, and they meet me at Loughborough on Thursday. Mr Bates desires his warmest thanks to you, and is now determined to go with us and I fancy we shall go south west the latter end of this or beginning of next week, nor can I tell where you can write to but Dishley, and the oftener the better. I dine with Mr Deverel today, stay all night and to Mr Thackers tomorrow to settle that account, so to Dishley again. You need not hurry about this bill until you be at Mark fair if this be with you before you send one. I wish E. Tulip happy and am with every good wish yours always
Goo Culley

PS This family joins with Mr Walker in compliments.
PS I am to have some more information respecting the price of wood. You have certainly made a good end so far of your fat cattle and sheep both store and fat, these Yorkshire men do well in drawing so much money from the north
8. Dishley Thursday 18th November 1784
Dear Brother

On Monday last I received a letter from you promising a bill soon of 40 or 50£ which letter I answered and sent from Nottingham on the Tuesday. Since then have been at Mr Deverels and Mr Thackers who paid me the ball 4£ 11s 6d so you may settle that account. The full ball was 4£ 11s 8d. Mr Thacker is a most respectable character, highly esteemed in his own neighbourhood, and said to be enlarging his fortune by a successful train of business. He can grind 100 quarter per week, but does 50 upon an average, is concerned in a cotton mill at the same place, which I was favoured with a sight of (I forgot to tell you that my friend T. Bates is gone to Woolsthorpe but we expect him and Mr Walker again today). This is an amazing piece of machinery totally inexplicable by me, but I can conceive it would have been a great feast to you Mr Matt: they employ above 50 children of both sexes and of different ages, who have one man to manage them in every room, the whole is an astonishing proof of mans inventive powers. The whole apparatus cost about 4000£. I am happy to tell you that there is one erected at Tedbury in Staffordshire, which is principally employed in spinning wool which though more difficult to spin than cotton, these gentlemen tell me there is not to doubt but in a few years there may be many employed in spinning wool. There is also a forge mill for rolling iron plates for tinning, much in the same stile as Mr Kendles above Warkworth, which gentleman I find is a native of Staffordshire and was concerned in the same manner, in that populous country, may probably have connections with his brothers who carry on similar works in Staffordshire. A woollen or fulling mill is also in this busy place, all upon the Derwent 8 miles from Derby 8 from Cavendish Bridge, a most eligible situation, because the canal that brings wheat &c to Mr Thackers mill, communicates with the Trent, Mersey, Severn and Thames and consequently with every sea that surrounds this wonderful island. Mr Thacker bought some of your kind of spring wheat while I was with him at 2 guineas per quarter. Wheat is dropping at present but Mr Thacker is so candid as to say, that he is quite of opinion that wheat will be higher sold in the spring and summer, from its being a much worse crop than people at first thought: it yields ill both to the flail and flour. If you please Sir
you may consider this information as coming from a respectable quarter. Barley he is not so clear about but is sure it will not be low, thinks it very likely to hold if not advance in price. Oats are sure to advance he says. We have had a succession of wet for many days, 8 at the least, and is very like to continue if we may judge from appearance, and if so we may retard if not quite stop our western tour. You may tell Mr Thompson of Lilburn, that I have not forgot him, that on asking Mr Bakewell he abruptly said he would sell none (bulls) and I have seen few besides that please me except for Mr Fowlers who will not sell a good one. Good long horns are in fewer hands than sheep, and they are not in many hands. Its amazing how fashions change, not many years ago nothing would do but short carcases and short legs, now they must be long carcased and stand high or they will not do at all, thin necked, straight topped, flat topped, and wide, in short light in the useless parts, and thick in the useful parts. I am talking of sheep Mr Matt, most people fond of size, hence you may trace the taste for the Durham sheep. Mr Deverels look sadly, but may answer for a few very large sheep. He has let his Durham tup for more than he cost. The very high prices Mr Bakewell has and may let at stagger all their neighbours, and what it will come to I know not but the higher he lets the better for those that have of the same family, and the higher the sheep will stand in credit. Mr Bakewell is gathering a vast quantity of haws, so I hope you will not neglect. He says people are tired of growing quicks, and probably will not be so keen again. Unavoidable delays always attend matters of consequence. Mr Bakewell cannot go until another week on account of some particular business, so I think we shall turn and be coming home unexpected. Had we thought of it, some of the sheep drivers coming to York might have come up for my two yearlings, for they will hinder us much on our return, as they cannot travel above 20 miles per day. I now repent that I allowed Mr Huskisson to buy them, indeed he would have kept them, but I could not do that with propriety. One good will attend it, the slow rate of travelling will suit our horses, not but they have stood the work well. Your horse still sweats, but not so much as he did, and keeps his condition well. We have had a very severe frost now for 2 days, after a great wet.

20th November . You have not told me but I hope you have examined all your tups and breeding sheep for yellowness? Mr Bakewell lost his credit entirely, he says, in one part of the south not to be retrieved, by a tup of his proving yellow, and getting yellow ones. It is of high import to attend to every outlet now. Old Rumps's sons are in higher credit than any others out of Mr Bakewells hands now, therefore I hope you will attend to them. Mr Walker says cabbage is the best to teach tup lambs to eat green food in the winter, they generally sink or lose condition before
they take to eat turnips properly. Tell William Atkinson to be sure all your sheep are well kept. In this country, they now do not keep their store ewes so well as they used to do in the autumn, but keep them better as they get heavier with lamb, as many have been lost in this country with many being in too great condition when lambing time came, but that is a complaint that ours have not the same chance to be lost by.

21 November . Mr Bates is in high favour with Mr Bakewell in consequence of his fondness for watering ground. Mr Bakewell always calls him Brother Bates . Wool I am told lowers in price in this part which I am sorry for. Mr Bakewells cabages are very good this year and his turnips tolerable. Lord Winchilsea was here yeaterday, a pleasing young nobleman, who talks of having some stock from Mr Bakewell. He has a seat in the southern part of this county. Have you sown any wheat at Cornhill? Has Brother James sown much? I hope you do not neglect to give your work oxen turnips along with their straw, remember how well they did with it last winter, and it is much cheaper feed than hay and I believe better for working or growing cattle. Do give all your young cattle a few turnips or shells with the straw. The Dishley people give cabbages, turnips, or carrots to all their cattle with straw sufficient to keep them open in the bodies. I see I have acted very foolishly in permitting Mr Huskisson to buy us those 2 yearlings, not only in being too high priced, but their inability to travel so far, when so young, and at so late a season, besides their staying at meat so long with Mr Bakewell is what I do not like on reflection, because it may be 6 weeks or more before we return, in short I am in ill humour with myself about these said horses, and yet for you to send a person on purpose for them will add still more to the price. However I shall leave this to you and William Browns consideration. Would old John Wright and his ass be able to fetch them? If anything should happen the poor old man by the way I should repent still the more, so I know not what to do, had it been summer it would have been no great matter, but now they must have hay &c. Pray help me to contrive some way to relieve me in this, in many respects seeming difficulty, I would think nothing of the trouble of taking them down in my hand only the eating Mr Bakewells hay &c. You see us two and 4 horses so long together is terrible and not easy kept. As to myself, I grow shamefully fat and cant help it without I should starve myself altogether. I am sure you would not know me? If a man comes for these 2 yearlings he should either have Jock Galloway or if he could be trusted to walk it would be better, but if he rides upon
either, he will kill them. They will travel 20 or 24 miles per day and any man may well walk that. He may lead one and the other will follow like a foal. They are shod before and he may have them done behind. We have been at Mr Huskissons again, Lord Wentworth, Mr Knowles's, Mr Creswells, Mr Salisburys (Goo), &c &c. And on our return this 24th November received a letter from my sister Jane, and finished by James, pray tell them I am particularly obliged and will as soon as possible answer them. In answer to yours Mr Matt I am glad the distillery is to go again, it will make a difference to the price of barley I have no doubt, and you will see by a part of this letter that barley rather mends in price in this country, it will also compel the factors to comply with the resolution respecting boll and score, in truth it makes little difference upon the whole, but I have not time to enlarge upon it now, Mr G. Logan will find it rather difficult to hire a good sheep at Dishley next season according to present appearances. I had rather Bill Gill has come here for a horse. The 2 Jameses have sold the 100 ewes well. I am sorry Mr Atkinson has missed the mountain. It is not enough that your lambs are clear of yellowness, you must examine your tups and tup lambs and breeding ewes &c &c. I am pleased with your hiring James Kerr and James Hewitt and I would not have you miss Andrew Laidlaw. We talk of going south on Friday first but would wish the bill here in the mean time. You will see what I have said about the horses above, and would have you do as seems best. If Lisle comes at all, he may as well come to Dishley, perhaps John Breedon will show him a little of the stock, let him have a letter from you to Breedon requesting a sight of such things as are agreeable to themselves, and as Mr Bakewell and we would probably be out Breedon will then rather show him things. Let him call at Wentbridge as I may possibly send them thither. I think May or in the spring better for Matt going to Mr Armstrong than now, but would wish you to speak to Mr Armstrong about it and take Matt with you if weather permit, you have all my thanks, and the Almighty will reward you for your attention to my children. I am exceedingly happy that Dr Kerr manages him so well. Pray God continue them good health and his Almighty Grace. As Matt thrives so well, he need have no bark, or I was thinking it might be right to give him a little bark and red port or the latter now and then may be better. Why does Nelly grow so thin? I hope she is allowed milk enough &c and puddings. Is not ripe fruit wholesome, I wish you and them had as many good apples and pears &c as we met with everywhere in this land of plenty. By a letter this day from Mr Stubbins I find Mr Pickering (William) has wrote to him lately and was so kind as to desire him to tell me, all was well with you. My thanks pray when you see him and compliments. You may depend on my calling at Denton on my return and lending every assistance in my
power to Messrs Hardcastle and Peacock. John Todd is in luck. I am sorry you were disappointed in not receiving my answer to your last but am sure it would not be far from Wooler at the time you mention, as I wrote immediately on receipt of yours and shall write as often as possible when out though you can only write here unless to Mr Bells London that married Nanny Atkinson, as I shall be there if we be in London, which we shall certainly be which ever way we go. But more of that in my next as I shall send this immediately. Mr Bates and everybody join in due respects with your ever offed
Goo Culley

PS I like the idea of Lisles coming for the 2 yearlings best because he will see the country and is able and I hope will be willing to walk with them 20 or 24 miles per day, but he must be charged not to ride upon any account as they cant bear it, but if he leads one the other will follow like a foal in a day or 2.
9. Dishley Thursday 25th November 1784
My kind friend and brother

Though I sent you a letter last night in answer to one from you, and one from Jenny and James, I must not omit acquainting you that I have this moment received Messrs Surtees and Burden draft on London at 40 days for 50£ for which you have my best thanks. Its money makes the mare to go Mr Matt: there is only one evil will attend the matter, like all children Master Thomas and I will be playing tricks when we get to London, and not get so soon home again as we ought to do. Mr Huskisson is luckily here this moment and I believe rather scant of cash, so I hope to get cash for my bill today and pay him for the horses. Mr Huskisson advises me to buy a stone horse, which his brother Sam has and which horse Sam bought in the mares belly at Dishley sale, says he will suit us to cover our own mares, and work, is the sort Mr Huskisson likes, and what we like, and supposes he will be bought for 30 guineas is well bred, and out of as good a mare as any that ever was at Dishley and got by G horse, but is almost blind. Now you must consult with Jenny, William and Bartholomew Brown on the matter, the quere with me is whether it is right to breed horses or not? If it is whether strong or light? Reason says strong ones in our situation are best, and indeed they pay the most
in all situations I believe. I hate stone horses to use as stallions in travelling the country &c but querie whether it is not right to have one for our own use? if it be right to breed at all, because it is clearly better to breed good or useful horses than unuseful, and it will prevent us from being plagued with other stone horses and their keepers coming about us. And perhaps the best farmers horses are bred from a black stallion (if not too clumsy) and country mares. You may be sure I shall not buy this horse or any other without the approbation of my friends nor until I see the horse and if I should buy him or any other before my return, it should make no difference in your sending Lisle or any other for the two yearlings because he would not bring the stallion with them for the stallion must I apprehend be led by himself. I am glad the Stones fair proved so good, and also that your receipts were good, as well as payments . The latter are always certain. Beef cattle are scarcely sold here at 4s per but mutton keeps 4d and tallow is 5d. I am with true regards Yrs
Goo Culley

Loughborough corn markets much the same. PS Buy Matt strong shoes or clogs, only I am afraid clogs would hurt his ankles. Mr Thacker has promised to give me cash for the bill. NB I believe we shall go south tomorrow if all be well, therefore if you hear nothing to the contrary may send a letter to Mr Bells that married Nanny Atkinson, my sister can give you a direction. I mean a letter directed to me at Mr Bells, as I shall be anxious to hear of you all. And if we once set forward it may be some weeks before we return.
10. Dishley 26th November 1784
Dear Matty

Mr Bakewell advises me, to have you direct to me thus (Mr Culley at Mr Honeyborns No 10 Throgmorton Street London) until you have advice to the contrary. Mr Honeyborn is his nephew, that we pronounce improperly Huniball, and says we shall stay in that part of London near Mr Honeyborns, and that he will send any letters after us, which may come to his hand, in case we should travel further south or west. By my writing you so many letters just now, you are not to expect Mr Matt: that you are to be plagued with so many every day or every week, no: I fancy when we once set forward we shall be so taken up with business or the contrary that we cannot write so often as you and we would wish, however you may be sure I will write as often as I conveniently can. Pray tell Mr Thompson of Lilburn that Mr Bakewell has a bull, which he would recomend to Mr Thompson as a particular good ox and heifer getter, is
of as good a sort as any they have, but I cannot prevail upon Mr Bakewell to take less than 15£ per season for 2 seasons, and not even so little as that except Mr Thompson will be at the expense of both fetching and taking back to Dishley. I believe this is the lowest that he will take, therefore Mr Thompson must judge for himself. I will endeavour to describe the bull. He is rather larger than the generality of the Dishley bulls, with very little coarse about him except his neck which is very leathery and coarse indeed, his rumps, hips, sides, and top all very good in my opinion, that is not so exceedingly wide, as kind to handle, very mellow in the touch indeed, and better flesh upon him than most bulls, perhaps as good as many oxen, his colour light red, and bone fine, in short if we were not too far from Mr Thompson, I should have no objection to join him in the hire, but perhaps Mr Thompson may get some of his neighbours to join him though B. Marshall may not, though I fancy Mr Marshall would like this better than the one they had from Dishley before. Yet he is far from catching except you feel, and then I think he will please a judge. But after all this recomending a stallion is only an unthankful office, and I would not have ventured to have said this much, if not to a Mr Thompson, or such like reasonable person, who would believe that I would not wilfully mislead them, I may err thorough ignorance but not intention. It appears strange and awkward to me, after being already 8 weeks from home, to set out upon a fresh journey, that may employ us almost 8 weeks more. But my friends have always been kind to me, and when I reflect that we were glad to spend a few days or weeks with this extraordinary man when we could scarce afford it, makes me scruple less to spend a little time and not a little money with this genius, now we can the better afford it. Besides he is so much more communicative now than in Ashworths administration, indeed there is nothing now scarce that he will not give a straight answer to. One thing though is not so well we are seldom trusted without a guard only I have the honour to be guarded in general by the old General himself, in short he will scarce let me be out of his sight. As to my friend Thomas he rises higher in his esteem every day, so that you see we are a kind of prisoners. But we are not to complain of this because everybody else are treated in much the same manner that come to this place, and few days without some company lords or peasants . This kind of management hinders us from gaining that information from the servants to which we dare not so well ask the superiors, and a shilling will often purchase a good deal from a domestic. Nor are we to blame this conduct when we are given to understand that his servants are not unfrequently inveigled away by people that come about Dishley. Even your friend Trigger is going to leave Mr Bakewell and its believed that some have enticed him away and you must not be surprised, if Fenton
people fall under some suspicion, not from Mr Bakewell but some others. However I cleared up that matter by asking Trigger, who declared he never heard of it before. I believe it had its origin from some nonsense Ned has talked after he returned to Dishley with the stallion from Fenton. If Lisle is not come away for the yearlings before this come to hand, could he not bring the tup cart with him to Mr Collings and take the 2 tups home, viz Dr Edwards and his, he could leave the cart and horse at Mr Collings till he return. I offer this for your consideration. Mr Tailor of Salton will keep his another season I fancy though you had not time to write to him and I am afraid he has not wrote to you, perhaps I may call on him as we return.

Newark on Trent 27th November . We left Dishley this morning, viz Mr Knowles of Nelson who is going with us into Lincolnshire, Mr Bates and self. Mr Bakewell was to meet us here as some business detained him an hour or 2, but he is not come and now 8 o'clock at night, but I suppose he will reach us tmorrow at Wragby. We propose going thorough Lincolnshire and Norfolk to Mr Youngs in Suffolk and so to London. The weather is most delightful, after 10 days rain and 3 sharp frosts. Mr Bakewell is much mortified at not being able to find my M.S. in Dishley house, suppposes it has been lent but not to some of his neighbours and not remembered who. However he is more vexed at it I believe than I almost ever saw him. So we cannot show it to Mr Young, but its perhaps as well. Pray Mr Matt if I can be of any service to any of our connections in London let me know, not that I suppose we shall stay many days there until we visit the famous Mr Ducats. Some people say Mr Bakewell will not be rich still, without he make 2000 per annum of the letting scheme and his stock in feeding &c and 500 of corn, because they say the riding expenses is 500 at least with sending out tups, housekeeping 500 I believe labour 500 at least I suppose more and rent 500, therefore without he makes more than 2000 he can save nothing. However if he don't save now he never will I think, because its unlikely that these times can hold long, and what a shocking thing it would be for him to fail a 2nd time, but I understand they are paying of and doing well and I hope he will do. You see Mr Matt I send but little waste paper though I have little to write about but in writing to a friend I have no notion of pinching. God bless you all says
Goo Culley
11. Wragby Lincolnshire 29 November 1784
Mr Matt

We were going to breakfast with Mr Codd, but Brother alias Professor Bates as Mr Bakewell calls him had hurt a toe a little which is subject to inflame in frosty weather, and as he has had it to plaster with beeswax and butter it has stopped us half an hour, which time I have stole to write. We left Dishley on Saturday and at Newark that night I put a letter in to the post for you. On Sunday at Lincoln viewing Minster and at church. Monday a fair at Lincoln with large show of cattle of every kind but one like Mr Sails sheep, and came here last night.

Louth 1st December. Yesterday morning we breakfasted at Mr Codds from thence to a Mr Joshua Walesbys a tupman who has a very good shearling of Mr Walkers of Woolsthorpe, got by a Dishley tup, and a very large tup of Mr Chaplins, as different from Mr Walkers as two sheep well can be. We went next to Mr Chaplins but were only allowed to see the cattle. Mr Chaplin was not at home nor son but the servants no doubt had their orders, indeed Mr Bakewell and Codd are very odious to this country breeders, and especially to Mr Chaplin who is at the head of them and whose stock is diametrically opposite to Mr Bakewells and that sort. Mr Chaplins dinner bell rang while there but we were not asked to dine so went to this place and put dinner and supper into one. I tire though of this sauntering about we shall be long of prosecuting our journey at this rate, to be sure Mr Bakewell moves slow and days are short, but expenses run high, for we live all on the public at the rate of no less than 10s per day. When shall I repay this Mr Matt? Mr Bakewell hires all his principal servants for 3, 4 or more years at once, says then that they are then more interested in your behalf than from year to year &c. I wish you would make some water roads, you can do that in soft wet weather, down by the ladies close side, all you have to do is make the water run as thin and as level and equal as you can, down the middle of the old road, the stuff thrown to both sides, make a good walk or riding path in particular times, you have many other places in Fenton which will answer well in this way, wherever the fall is not too rapid. I beg you may make some trials upon a small scale at first when the places cut much a few stones can be put in but do not that too hastily as time will teach you and the sand washing in often does the job. A wash road must be quite contrary to a raised one, because the washed one must be hollow and troughed. The weather is rather wet again but fresh and good upon the whole.

2 December. This night at Swinhop Mr Walesbys a tupman where we also saw a rabit fold taken. They go at 8 at nights, they close the fold on the side next the burrows, the nets having been set on 3 sides before,
then the warrener and some assistants attend all night or else the rabbits eat their way thorough the nets, as soon as light in the morning all hands and dogs to work, when the poor rabbits are hunted down or into false holes where they afterwards take them out, from 100 to 500 couple are taken at different times. A snow has fallen in the night prevented the rabbits from resting so that few were taken.

December 3. All night at Mr Richard Codds who lives at Wikeham a good house and 300 per annum belongs to your friend Mr Harrison of Walworth. Mr Codd says it is dear, was valued by Butler. Torrington is the other estate belonging to Mr Harrison, which Mr Codd tells me is better land than this. Some good ground here but as I have not yet seen it, I cannot say what it is in general. Mr Codd takes it upon account of the house as he is a very independent man, married Mr John Codds sister who was a widow and has no children by him. As your brother and my friend Mr Thomas Bates is not much better of his toe, though no worse, yet can't prosecute his journey with that pleasure he would wish, so has determined all at once to return north, consequently I have not leisure to say all I could wish at present. It is totally uncertain when we get to London, or when I return, we get very slowly forward indeed, days so short, and people so kind. I do assure you we live well only too well Mr Matt. All the care I can take I can't keep from getting too fat. God bless you all my best respects to all and believe me ire affty
Goo Culley
PS I shall leave this open for Mr Bates to fill up as I have no secrets.
Hilton December 13th 1784
Dear Brother

Mr George was so kind to leave this letter for me to fill up and send from Newcastle, but being so anxious to get home I forgot the letter having a very sore toe or chilblain which I am very subject to in winter, which was the cause of my return northward so soon, which I submitted to with great reluctance from the very agreeableness of my journey with so good and intelligent company. I am apt to think would not have minded if I had continued my journey from the different manner of living that I am accustomed too, I am greatly obliged to you for the great respect you payed me in your brothers letters, and only wish that I may always merit your respect please to remember me to my dear sister and I should be happy to be under her care as surgeon. My mother was speaking about coming to Fenton but from a slight cold she has got and the inclemency
of the season she thinks it may be some time first, we are quite blown up with snow the roads impossible in may places so that the tups cannot come according to appointment but I hope to hear from you soon when you will fix another time, and when you send would be obliged to you for a few cuttings of your tree willow. My mother and brother joins me in complements to the whole family and am dear Sir with great respect yours sincerely
Thomas Bates
NB I purpose being at Fenton as soon as I can bear a boot upon my foot if it had been any way tolerable perhaps might have been the bearer of this letter.
12. Manby Mr Codds 4 December 1784
Dear Matty

Our friend Thomas left me at Mr R. Codds yesterday morning, and I sent a half finished letter by him. We meet with uncommon civility, among these hospitable gentleman breeders who to be men of so much good sense, its truly amazing that they should be so ignorant of good stock, and that they should have so long stuck to such useless stock, but the batle is now over they now give up to better judgement, this truly great and indefatigable man Mr Bakewell convinces in general wherever he goes, how much does his country owe him! But his merit will never be truly known, until he be dead I have often said.

5th December Tunby Swan - an od house, but a very good inn I assure you, fish beef and apple pie &c with nuts and apples after dinner are comfortable things on a bad snowy day. Mr Codd and I parted with Mr Bakewell yesterday, and went to a fen farm of his where we saw his tup hogs large and fat indeed going among cole or rape in this flat wet country by the Within which is made navigable between Gainsborough and Boston. We staid last night at Billinghay a large village upon the fen, and then this morning early went to Thickby Mr Fishers where we saw an ox heavier and perhaps still be made heavier than Mr Hills, a milk white, both sire and dam came from Teesside but Mr Fisher had forgot the mans name, he is I think the heaviest ox I ever saw, and very good points in general bones small, but not so very complete as Mr Hills was.
