We saw several good short horned cattle in this quarter, bred from Teeswater cattle. We crossed the Within again by Tattershall, a fine flat country to
this place Mr Fishers is near Sleaford another market town. I am to meet Mr Bakewell in the morning at Spilsby. I was witness to Mr Codd hiring the tup he has this season at 60, for 100 the next to tup 80 ewes only for Mr Codd, and 20 for Mr Bakewell before he leaves Dishley. What do you think of such work Mr Matt. I rejoice at it for my part and wish the old boy his health to play these pranks for years to come, it will be better for us and those near akin to him beside it will keep Mr Logan or at any rate he must pay a great price, if he comes another year and will have a good one, or anybody else, as for us I think its prudent to feel how we are a while before we give 100 guineas.

7th December A very snowy morning and much wet had fallen in the night, so that the fen country is much of it covered with water. Breakfasted with Mr Stevenson steward to Sir Joseph Banks, who was abroad with Capt. Cook, lives at Reesby in this neighbourhood and is president of the Royal Society. From hence to Spilsby with a market today. Monday Here I met with Mr Bakewell again and parted with Mr Codd. Met with a London drover who came on to London on Friday and says the market is bad 4s per stone sunk and 4 sink for sheep. Tuesday 8 December . Another wet morning, it has now rained and snowed most of 3 day days and nights. Waters are very much out and increasing, they talk of some of the banks having given way, a thing noways uncommon in these fenny countries, and does great damage when that happens, however we are in safe and good quarters at Mr Wrights Spilsby, and I assure you will not stir until we can do it with propriety. Mr Wright is a young man of a pretty fortune, natural son to a Mr Wright who is dead. His mother lives with him, and is much fatter than Mrs Moody. This is the Mr Wright who hired the tup called Shoulders which sheep Mr Logan bid 60 guineas for, he is a very nice sheep indeed, little but firm proportions light shin and pelt like paper, is now I may say rather very fat after serving 7 score ewes and being sunk in condition by being put in a poor pasture from the 20th of July to the time he was put to the ewes. Mr Bakewell says Mr G. Logan shall not have him under 120 guineas for his ride next season so Mr Logan may expect to be well done over if he comes to Dishley. Give me leave to explain Mr Bakewells mode now it is in my head in the tup way. He shows his tups (at least those fit to be seen) as soon as they come home from their rodes, to the 1st of June, then they clip and show none for 8 days, then on the 8th of June they exhibit them
stripped and show the let and unlet sheep until the 20th of July when they show the unlet ones no more but put them into a poor pasture until they go to the ewes, by this mode they are better able to do business, and peoples thoughts are not taken of the unlet ones by seeing the let ones. These methods strike at the roots of the Lincolnshire breeders, for theirs are never fit to be shown until near Michaelmas. But the battle is over in Lincoln and they have nothing to say now against Mr Bakewells sort only the wool, and that is now confessedly better than Lincolnshire in quality not 2 lb a fleece less weight in short the wool buyers prefer the Leicestershire and Mr Bakewell and his kind have a fine field before them indeed. I almost wish to be fixed in this fertile country. Mr Codd let 150 tups last season and made 930£ of them this is from his own mouth. Its like a new creation nay I am of an opinion that a Lincolnshire breeder would sooner come at his point by breeding from honest ewes than from their own, for I think no country can show such bad ones. This is the same Mr Wright that has Mr John Charges bull, is now 9 years old and in my opinion exceeds the bull John Lax has in some particulars, indeed this young man has it in his power to make a great figure in the breeding line. You must remember Mr Matt that the said tup Mr Wright has is brother to your shearing tups, as well as Cambrells, and of a most valuable sort I think, therefore pray proper attention to them and your tup lambs, for they are worth attending to they are now in fashion and will not soon go out I think for the principles are founded upon reason and true judgement it is like building a house upon a rock. God bless you all says ire offed brother
Goo Culley

PS You may be sure I long to hear from you, but must wait till we get to London. We make way very slowly as the sailors say. Mr Wright is to go with us for a few days, perhaps to London. I hope my friend T. Bates is near home by this, I gave him a letter to fill up and put into the post at Newcastle as he passed there. Mr Burns shepherd bought a tup at Leicester of the Dishley folk during the interregnum at 60 guineas and all the best sheep Mr Bakewell has are got by him, so much for Dishley blood, this information from Mr Wright, who hired of them from Mr Bourn before he knew Dishley.
13. Spilsby 8th December 1784
Mr Matt

I sent you a letter from this place this day, and as we are confined here
with bad weather, I cannot do better than employ a part of my time in writing to you believing that you will be willing to pay postage for my nonsense mixed with some perhaps useful intelligence. 9th December At Boston last night, where we sent for poor old Raynor formerly a tupman that used to bring tups to Milton, has fallen very poor, lost an eye and teaches school 2 miles from hence, and I am sure Mr Matt that you will not be angry at my giving him 1/2 a guinea and Mr Bakewell the same. We made the poor old man happy and felt pleased ourselves. This an amazing rich country I now have seen the land that carries nay makes fat an ox and 4 or 5 sheep per acre it is rich indeed, and when we consider the very bad kind of sheep it makes it more wonderful. However Mr Bakewell is like to reap a rich harvest in this country, and indeed they are coming over faster than one would imagine. Pray Brother keep these confused letters of mine together for my satisfaction and use, as I am unable to write a journal and letters to you must take care of these I beg. We are now at Holbeach a small market town outside the Wash or lost dike Wash, a small disagreeable place indeed, a road I shall not venture again I think, our guide rode with a long pole to grope or feel the road for fear of inlets or seeks where horses are sometimes lost and rider in imminent danger. Very lately a man lost his horse and escaped himself with some difficulty. This country fitter for geese and ducks than people and indeed we are not to wonder at its being so thin peopled though amazing full of stock they say unless they stock very hard they spoil the ground and that the land at Long Sutton is much worse since old Wallets time for want of stocking harder. They say sheep will not do upon old dead grass or what they call fog. At Boston they have bored 340 feet without meeting with water and are determined to persevere a little longer as fresh water is a blessing unknown here except what is catched from rain.

Sutton 10th December . A heavy snow having fallen last night, has prevented our viewing the richness of the land of this first grazing country perhaps in this island, where the famous Wallet made so much noise his descendants are likely to come to beggary. 'Sic transit gloria mundi'. Mr Wileman a very spirited clever man who now lives where Mr Wallet did live has 2 rams from Mr Bakewell this year. Mr Wileman tells me that a considerable quantity of wheat has lately been bought here to go abroad, but where to he knows not, so high as 50s per quarter some say to Ostend, but that is conjecture. This price for wheat is the more remarkable as it is higher than in the inland counties, for at Loughborough it was only
45s. I can form no idea of these prices standing, but shall tell you more when I hear of it respecting corn, oats 8s per comb, no barley grown here. Course of crops in general beans and wheat alternately without fallow. The spring wheat is taking place, they sow their beans broadcast. 11th December Long Sutton. It has been a most astonishing frost indeed but I have no doubt of you and William Brown and all the Privy Council doing to the best of your knowledge. I hope you have sold more of your ewes and other sheep, it is always generally right to sell for a fair profit, I am very happy you sold your cattle so near, I never think wintering cattle pay like sheep. I hope your oil cakes are arrived safe they are not to be bought under 5£ 15s and 6£ here. It is said barley is much dipped at Lynn and to the south: I do not understand this, when wheat is advancing. The wheat I mentioned is going to America (Nova Scotia) I believe.

Sunday 12th December Wisbeach. This is a considerable town much corn comes down the Nen, and is principally bought by a Mr Baker of Lynn whose clark Mr Donkin is a Morpeth man and he and I got acquainted. They do a deal of business to Leith and up the Firth to Mr Steins and know all our corn merchants &c. Indeed this is a most fertile country all the Isle of Ely is I am told, some land keeps from 5 to 10 sheep per acre in the summer and near a beast per acre to keep it down, also generally a horse in every piece of 7 or 8 acres which they think does little harm. The graziers and farmers are a genteel sensible intelligent sort of men, drink wine like water, very expensive I assure you, seem to have read much, and in general well bred. They tell me that Mr Mewburn has realized 800 per annum . Planting wheat costs 10s per acre 5 pecks per acre do not hand hoe, only dibbled upon clover lees what they call flag, put it in about 2 or 2 1/2 inches deep, 2 rows upon a flag or furrow 9 inches wide and as flat as possible, they plow 4 inches deep. This information from a Mr Saffray who prefers Gilsthorps plows to the wheelplow, says nothing but custom can authorise the wheelplows.

Lynn Regis 13th December . We are just arrived here, and as Mr Bakewell had ordered his London letters to meet him at this place, I was in hopes of a letter also, but I could hardly expect it there has not been time, but I hope to be gratified with a letter when we reach London which I fancy will be this week about Sunday. We have been all last night with a Mr Thistleton at Walpole a village in Marshland 5 miles on this side Wisbeach. We have been 3 days in travelling 19 miles indeed the weather has been very winterish. Marshland properly so called, consists of 7 towns or parishes, all very rich land except the fen part which is untrained, and produces only reeds and other aquatic weeds with which they thatch their houses uncommonly neat thorough all this rich flat country, which in all probability has all been got from the sea at different periods, prodigious
quantities of wild ducks, teals and other fowls are decoyed or shot in these fens and sent to London also many eels and tench and pike caught. They have a common here called Marshland Smee said to be preferable to Sutton common, carries in summer, I am credibly informed 10 of the large long wooled Lincolnshire sheep per acre, besides many young cattle and horses, indeed we have rode over a tract of country from a little on this side of Spilsby to Lynn of near 40 miles extent besides it extends along the Lincolnshire coast northward, and up to Peterborough westward, and southward into Cambridgeshire Huntingtonshire and some say thorough Essex to the Thames, which is so flat that I suppose a few feet of water would cover the greatest part of it and so rich as is not easily conceived, those parts excepted which lye so low that the water is not or cannot well be got of and are called fens or lows from 4 to 10 sheep per acre beside cattle in summer and 1 1/2 sheep per acre in winter. But thorough all this tract of county the sheep and cattle are in general (I mean the country breed) of the very worst quality and worth the least per lb of any other part of the kingdom that I know of. At crossing a place called Germans Bridge 4 miles from this town over the river that comes to Lynn the stock immediately change, from Lincolnshire sheep and cattle you come at once to Norfolkers, from the longest wool to near the shortest and in many other respects very different. Now they cannot both be right for the same kind of land, it's a quere with me if either are right. Mr Donkin is of opinion that barley and other grain, wheat excepted will drop in price, barley I understand has fallen most rapidly within these last 10 days in the southern part of this island, therefore perhaps you had better sell what barley you have thrashed or in hand, though one does not know, if they come to export much it may make a material difference in a few weeks. Mr Bakewell desires to join in good wishes with your ever offed
Goo Culley

PS I forgot to tell you that turnips are a very good crop in this country I am told, but will be able to tell you more of this in my next. Fat cattle fell in price at Boston fair last Saturday and at some other fairs lately, London market bad, indeed I should not wonder if this weather putting in so severely does not hasten many people to market that would have put of a few weeks, some people are afraid of turnips going with the frost, but I hope you have more snow to cover yours.
14. Lynn 13th December 1784

I sent you a letter from hence last night, and this is a very coarse day indeed. Business is done here in the corn buying way in the readiest and most methodical manner I ever saw, the factor takes his stand, and the farmers present their samples in paper bags, he bids always within 5s per last (all combs and lasts here) generally only bids once, except the sample is of good quality, if the farmer accepts the offer, the buyer takes it and bag, and puts into his pocket but first, sets down with a pencil the quantity in lasts and combs, the price per last and sellers name, but what I was most pleased with, was a little poor boy or girl standing by every buyer with a spread apron to catch the corn that fell from the merchants hand as he was viewing the samples, so that nothing is lost and in the numerous samples that here are exhibited, more is saved than you would imagine. Astonishing quantities of barley, and a good deal of wheat are shown in this busy market, several white peas and some rye. They begin about 12 o'clock and at one the bell rings and everybody go to dinner. The barley is ill coloured and thin this year sold from 11 to 12£ per last, wheat from 21 to 24£ per ditto , white peas 15 to 17£, oats 7 to 8£ 8s per last, 21 combs are allowed for 20 always and in all grain. The oats very bad in quality and few shown, they are called short smalls very improperly, for they are long smalls, I know not what kind they are, but suppose them a bad kind of Dutch oats, wheat and barley the great exports. I am told that more corn is exported from Yarmouth, however a very great deal is shipped from hence, more than from any port I am acquainted with. The market place is a fine square, on the north side the cross and shambles form a crescent, behind them stand cattle and pigs and a Dr Yeldall a quack doctor before upon forms stand first, the Marshland butter, eggs, poultry &c in 2 rows then the Norfolk butter &c then in the open area stands the factors and farmers. Except the market place this town consists of narrow streets like most ports, but covers a large space and has been fortified by a mote and wall.

(15 December Wednesday). Still frosty and likely to continue, we are now at Castle Rising an ancient borough, 4 miles to the left of Lynn, near the sea. We have altered our rout for the present, and if the weather hold shall not go to London now because our motive was to visit Mr Ducats, but if this frost continues we cannot see Mr Ducats management, however you may still write to London until you have my orders to the contrary, because we may go to London nevertheless if the weather change, after we have visited Norwich &c which is our present plan. A Mr Faucet who is mayor of this old borough has 2 tups of Mr Bakewell this season and where we now are.

(Thursday 16th December ). We left Mr Faucets hospitable mansion thorough Dessingham and Tring to Somerfield a very excellent farm a Mr Curtis's who Mr Young mentions in his Tour. This gentleman has excellent conveniences and plows 1000 acres. barley, wheat and turnips with clover is the common practice, but it is amazing how few cattle they winter here, upon straw in short the straw is in a great measure wasted. This country is in general poor land and appears to be tiring of the plow, many heaths in the days ride. From Mr Curtis's to Mr Wrights where we saw some Norfolk sheep, a very middling sort to me. We now passed through Burnham to Holkham, but unfortunately Mr Coke is from home. The general practice of feeding turnips I find is by pulling the turnips around the hedges and making lanes or roads thorough the piece, which are taken either to cattle in the folds or in grass fields to plow next spring, the remainder they eat with sheep upon the ground, then always plow 3 times and sow 3 bushels of barley with 10 or 12 or some 16 lb clover and only 1/2 a peck rye grass but is very careful to have good seed and pure rye grass, a little trefoil and white clover also when meant for pasture. They plow in both wheat and barley, the wheat mostly in stitches or 2 plow bouts, mow barley and reap the rest. It is truly astonishing to see almost a whole country under the plow and in general well done, they generally plow 2 and 3 acres in summer all use wheel plows here and say they cannot plow so much with any other plows. I was mistaken in thinking they soiled horses in the summer, but I think they are wrong in not doing it. They chain their horses in the stable by the forefoot to the manger posts instead of tying by the head, an odd way this I think.

Friday 17th December . We this morning after viewing the elegant house and sumptuous furniture of Mr Cokes at Holkham, his horned and polled sheep, with the idea of imparking 10 miles circuit of ground, the richest service of plate they say in this island and the bed where the Prince of Wales slept a few nights ago, passed through a well cultivated country to Fakenham, a small market town, and 1/2 a mile further at the Kings Head Hampton dined (an ordinary inn) and just by the famous
Hampton Green where the Scotsmen annually sell many thousands of Galloway and West Highland cattle. The fair begins the 22nd of November and continues until all are sold, many are now unsold especially one Moffat from the border of Airshire who sells vast numbers. The weather setting in so severe is against my countrymen but they die hard, and sell their cattle very high indeed. An old genius called John Stone who has kept the market 43 years knew me by being once in my company along with Mr Thorne, who tells me Mr Thorne died last March. From here to Dereham a pretty market town 14 miles a woodland country ill cultivated most of the way. This country like many others seems only well cultivated in particular places, indeed I have not so very high an opinion of this promontory as I had. Their great forte is the plow, but they have the worst way of converting that straw into manure I have anywhere seen, and as to stock of most kinds, they are totally ignorant, they use their sheep only as carriers of manure from one field to another. We propose for Norwich in the morning from whence I intend to send this, and would have you write no more to London as I think we shall turn to the north again from Norwich to Bury where we have ordered our letters to meet us from London, for it means nothing going to the metropolis or Mr Ducats this season, this season when we cannot view the country for snow. If the weather should change we may still change our minds and go further south, but of that you should have notice if we go. You may still write to Dishley because though I shall not stop much there yet it will be a while before I reach that place I suppose as we travel very slow, Mr Bakewell being unable to make much sail. Bumps I mean my horse has a good time of it which will enable him I hope to stand work better after, his legs swell a little at nights but nothing to signify. I hope you will let me know how my friend T. Bates is, Professor as Mr Bakewell says, I am very anxious to hear of you I confess, having heard nothing now of some weeks, but I hope the best. I beg you will tell my sister Jane Culley that I am sorry I have not found time to compose her and James letters but I am sure you will excuse me, when I assure her that I have not leisure, for we are so engaged in conversation &c &c that I have barely time to scrawl these letters to you, and I hope you let all my friends see these letters that choose, as I have no secrets nor wish for none. It's a long time to be absent from my children but I consider them in the best of hands, who with them have my prayers and I trust will ever have my grateful thanks. We have in this country 4 or 5 inches of snow but when we were near the sea at Holkham we had no snow. At this place we have met with our quack doctor again, brother in law to Dr Green.

18th December . We arrived at this populous place to breakfast,
and a view of the market, an amazing quantity of provisions, astonishing number of people, but the corn market is smugled, and not done openly and methodically like Lynn, the streets narrow and very close built, said to contain 40000 people, the manufactory flat in what they call Norfolk stuffs. This day and last night soft and inclined to rain, but as the wind keeps easterly I think it will draw to frost again. As the post goes out in an hour or less and we are just going to dine must conclude by wishing the compliments of the season and every other good wish to all the Culleys and connections and am yrs &c
Goo Culley
15. Norwich Sunday
Dear Jenny

I was much obliged to you, for your kind attention in writing me a few lines. I hope you will accept my sincere thanks for the indulgence you and Matty have given me, it will be my duty to make a proper return. I wrote to Fenton yesterday, which letter I expect all my friends to see for I have no secrets. I am glad you have got so well forward in business, and have sold so many of your fat stock &c. Markets have been long overloaded and this weather will make them more so yet. Mutton is sold everywhere that we have been at 4 d and 4 1/2d per lb. For particulars I refer to my letter to Matty yesterday and am with true regard to my sister and the Nellys your ever offed

Goo Culley
PS I feel for you in this hard weather but am glad to hear that you have so much snow as it will save turnips &c. As soon as we reach Bury shall turn north. Except the weather turn frosts and I may be tempted to go see Mr Ducats management but much will depend on the letters from Matty, however I would not have Matty write any more to London until he hears from me again, but to Dishley.
16. Norwich 19th December 1784
Dear Brother

I sent you a letter on Saturday from this place, and one to my sister yesterday. We dined with the famous Watson, who formerly lived at Ellerton near Catterick in Yorkshire, and now practises farriery in this large city. He is vain but clever, and reprobates the gambling life, in short he is an odd compound, and succeeded to a Mr Clover who was most eminent in his profession, and has retired from business with 10000£. There are 34 parish churches, besides a French one, and many meetings of various sects. The river Yare runs though the midst of the town, and is navigable for small craft from Yarmouth which is 20 miles from it. A very large market indeed, and the farmers, and farmers wives come in market carts, many hundreds of them, and bring not only poultry, and butter and eggs, but veal, pork, and mutton, killed by them and retailed here. A man last night robbed 3 or 4 of these carts as they returned home, at last a rough farmer comes up and said D-n you Sir I'll lose my life before my neighbour shall be robbed, he immediately seized the fellow, though he had a brace of pistols, tied him put him into his cart, and brought him back to Norwich in triumph, where he now lies in irons.

Stratton 12 miles south of Norwich Monday 20th December . We are now bound for Ipswich, as Mr Bakewell would see the famous Suffolk Punch horses. We have had 2 days softish but no thaw, for the country is covered with snow as soon as you leave this city. They pay 8d in the £ poor cess, and this once flourishing manufactory is now said to be on the decline, in short we are told that Yorkshire and Lancashire are stealing the trade from both the west and east of England. The cattle in this country are polled duns in general and I conceive them to be bred from the Galloway cattle as they are very small but not as true made as the latter. The country on both sides this city is divided into small enclosures, which appears to have been done many years as the trees are old pollards in the hedgerows, the management the same as in every part of Norfolk, the plow is their forte , stock they seem totally ignorant of, and it is amazing that in a country where so much straw is grown that they should
not breed more cattle. I suppose they buy more Scots into this country than any other in England, they firkin butter but sell it at only 26s per firkin. We saw Mr Coke of Holkham at Norwich, a very agreeable man, but lost his election for the county by being a Foxite. Mr Bakewell gives his ewes and other sheep barley straw in hecks, on turnips, when hay is scarce, and always recomends hay to hogs at turnips, or other sheep, or some dry meat.

Scale End. We this day left Harlestone a few miles to the east of us, another great fair for Scotch cattle, which they call the finishing fair, it was removed from Hoxam a few years ago. Woolpit is in Suffolk and I had always been led to believe that it was in Essex. We are now among the Suffolk chestnut horses, a very useful kind I think, though their legs are round and fleshy, but no hair, backs not wide, but a deal of belly, and horses with a belly are often hard and of a good constitution. We saw a stallion near 16 hands, cost 76£ yet not so good as some geldings and mares which we have seen. This inn is 20 miles from Norwich, 23 from Ipswich, 23 from Bury, 23 from Thetford and 20 from Beccles, a very good house indeed. Stoneham pie in the vale 1/2 mile, we cross a small river by a wooden bridge into Suffolk and a little further by mistake we get to Eye a small market town, but soon get right again and about 6 o'clock arrived at this inn, a very cold frosty night.

Stonhampie 21st December . We slept all night with the Revd Mr Philip Toosey who is going to Canada by the appointment of Government, with his family and servants. I am to write by him to William Cleghorn. We have seen several Suffolk horses, they are sorrels with white faces in general, shoulders too forward thin girth thick bellied, short quartered, and round legged, yet they are said to be good drawers and hardy, which may be for thick or deep bellied horses are often of a good constitution. They soil many of their horses in this country. Many cabbages are grown here but of a much inferior sort to Mr Bakewells. I wish I may remember to buy some cabbage seed before I return from Dishley. We passed thorough Stowmarket and Woolpit where the great fair is for short horned cattle in the latter end of September and is in this county though I always imagined it was in Essex. Still quite an enclosed country with many oak trees, and the most pollards I ever saw.

Bury 22nd December . Came here this morning in a very heavy snow. Market day, some cattle (Suffolks) and very shabby. Barley 20 to 22s per
quarter rather a better price for good than had been of 2 weeks. This is a very large clean town, much long wool brought here from Lincolnshire, combed and spun, and sent in yarn to Norwich and London while most of their own wool goes to Yorkshire, this seems very odd but so it is. Was very happy to receive a letter from you here by way of London being the first of near a month. However I am happy, very happy to hear you are all well, as to the weather never mind as long as you have no hay down that is we must be content always with what pleases God to send us, it is same for you as other people, not but I long much to be with you, to lend you my feeble aid, it is now 3 months this day since I left Fenton, and when I get back I know not, we travel so slow I am quite tired, but I cannot help it as I cannot leave Mr Bakewell until we get to Dishley, which I hope will now be in 6 or 8 days, as we turn north tomorrow after seeing Mr Young. I am glad you have got so much wheat sown, Mr Alder is rather light but perhaps he dare not act otherwise. I forgot to tell you Mr Young like others is no prophet in his own country, and its said he is going to drop his monthly publication I believe you are right Mr Matt short thick carcases are best, thick on the top. I am glad you have gathered some haws, and also that you are going to plant cabbages and turnips for seed, but I am afraid the snow has catched you. I am glad you keep sending to Crosbe better sell for little profit than be left for turnips. Snow is a blessing in that light to save your turnips. You say nothing of oil cakes, I am afraid they wont come. Pox on Mr Walkers dinmonds they are unlucky, but never mind do the best to your knowledge and all will go right. When lambs lose their lies as Rumps's did last spring they seldom or never recover it therefore cannot look well. I am afraid the remittances from America will be uncertain by all accounts but how have you paid your March rents if you have got no money from Starforth. Its certainly right to give your work oxen and all your young cattle a few turnips along with straw for a thousand obvious reasons. I am happy very happy surely to hear of my childrens welfare, and I am particularly obliged to you for your attention to my boy and his clogs I wish my sister would allow Nelly more liberty, but I hope she will as I wrote to her about my girl from Norwich. Children and all young animals are fond of liberty, plain wholesome food and plain whole clothes are clearly right to me. Mr Matt keep Matt whole and as plain as you will, make up some more of my old clothes for him when he wants for they will be of no use to me. I wish much to be at home to live poorly for we live so well and do so little it is impossible
but to grow fat. T. Bates got fat well my off. I blame you not for Alex Weightman going away, only stick to the Browns, and you will do for the rest. R. Davison may do very well. It was a fortunate event that Crosbe &c sold all his cows, and that you have so few fat cattle for wintering, I think nothing of sheep compared to cattle, and I find most people say that cattle pay less in general for wintering upon turnips than sheep, as to wintering a few for summer grazing upon straw and a few turnips a different affair. The quantity of Irish cattle that are come over and may make a difference in the spring, as to prices, the Scots are hard with the Galloway cattle now in hand in this country, and will lose by them I am told. We saw the terrible accounts of the loss by sea newspapers, it is very odd by the papers, the snow has fallen on almost every part of this island but where we have been, for 4 or 5 inches deep here and no drifts, very decent riding, only we walk. I do not remember that I said much to Mr Barugh about from done it for the best poor man, and we especially I must be care matters, indulgent brothers hurt me I believe. As the post goes shall conclude with every good wish your offed
Goo Culley
PS I am afraid the weather would catch my friend T. Bates you say nothing of him.
17. Bury 23 December 1784
Mr Matt

I sent you a letter yesterday from this place after receiving yours of the 4th and 7th inst. I also wrote to you from Norwich and to my sister, from Lynn, from Spilsby or Boston I forget which, and from Newark, and Dishley, and have only received yours of yesterday. But I am content and happy as I had a good account. I only now fret that I am unable to assist you, in this critical season, and when I shall reach you I know not, for we move slow indeed. We breakfasted yesterday with Mr Young, who wishes much to have the sending of my manuscript into the world, but his own writings and deeds are in such bad repute that Mr Bakewell will not allow me to trust it to him, saying that everything that comes through
Mr Youngs hands will appear to disadvantage, such bad credit are his writings in his own country. And indeed when we consider it is not to be wondered at, people that devote their time to writing cannot act or execute. His sheep are scabbed, his cattle ill chose and worse managed, in short he exhibits a sad picture of mismanagement. We viewed Sir Charles Davers's flock, they are rather better than the general run, but they never can be right with narrow sharp tops, and thin sides. I have had quite enough of this. We dined at a Mr Simons, along with 3 French men one a count, 3 courses with candlelight, sad work, only plenty of apples by good luck.

24 December . Mr Young came to us to breakfast at the Bell this morning and took us to a Mr Pricks where we saw 11 rams, then to Mr Wrights who has very nice conveniences, and a number of cattle feeding upon turnips. We now turned to the left to Barrow where Mr Macro made us very welcome to an excellent dinner &c &c. A fine fellow this lives like a prince, he farms 1200 acres. We saw 12 tups here measured the horns of one 36 inches long, and 9 1/2 round at the root, takes in cattle to straw at 6 per week. We staid all night, Mr Young with us, and breakfasted next morning Xmas day at Mr Mures a Scotsmen who made a fortune with the famous Atkinson in the contracts upon rum &c in Lord North's administration. However Mr Mure of Saxham is much of a gentleman, is retired from business and feeds 120 cattle of all nations upon turnips and cabbages tied up, has a machine to weigh them alive, which he does when put up and when intended to be sold. Here Mr Young left us, a man of the quickest conception I ever remember meeting with, but perhaps too precipitate, have you taken his Annals? Mr Macro conducted us to Dallam to Mr Houghtons who bought a horse of Mr Toosey bred by Mr Bakewell middling only. We dined and parted with the hospitable Macro, who I hope we have converted, at least he intends to visit Mr Bakewell along with Mr Young in March. Much is to be done in these horned countries but when I know not, the change is so very great that people cannot easily reconcile their ideas to a long wooled sheep with a thick carcase, who have been used to their deer kind of sheep, the more they approach to deer, the more lean flesh and less fat in proportion but more gravy of the claret kind Mr Matt. Mr Bakewell and I have recommended this consequently gentlemen's mutton and the manufacturers mutton are of two kinds, the one lean with gravy, the other fat with oil, the gravy meat open greened and porous, the fat meat fine greened and close. A Norfolk man says a sheeps horns should come out forward and turn in such a measure as you shall see the ears through or behind the horns. A Wiltshire breeder says
on the contrary that a sheeps horns shall come out backwards so that the ears may be seen before the horns, but a Sussex man says they are both wrong, for a sheep ought to have no horns. I forgot to observe that the Norfolk man is for a black face and legs, a Wiltshire white face and legs and Roman nosed, and a South Downs or Sussex breeder no horns and grey face. (We are charged 3s 6 for a fowl and 6d more for toasted cheese, and 6d for fire, but we are at Newmarket Sir.) It's a Suffolk man who says a sheeps face should be speckled.

Sunday 26 December . This morning we left Newmarket and breakfasted at Cambridge, where we paid 1s a piece and 3d per horse hay, this the highest I was ever charged, a dear country indeed, though a very fruitful one. From hence we turned aside to St Eves, as the market and show of cattle is tomorrow, only a small place in a flat country full of willows, the river Ouse brings up coals from Lynn and is navigable to Bedford I believe. Monday 27 December . Saw St Eves market about 200 sheep and 80 cattle, none good, but I am told this is one of their smaller markets and so it might being the first after Christmas. 7 miles to Huntington famous for Cromwells birth. We passed Godmanchester, and 1/2 a mile from Huntington is Hinchinbrook seat of Lord Sandwichs, his Lordship very civil, gave some beef, ale and wine. 12 1/2 miles to Stilton where we stop for this night. I forgot to tell you that 2 miles on yon side Cambridge is a single house called Sturbidge where the famous fair is held, its said a single peddler happened to set down his pack in harvest and they thronged so about him that the following year many more came which was the beginning of this fair, which is now like most others of that kind much declined. (28 December ). Breakfasted at Wansford in England an excellent house indeed, from thence to Stamford, one part in Lincolnshire and rest in Northamptonshire. We now left the great road, to Oakham in Rutlandshire, where we slept. Just by this place stands Burleigh, a well situated seat of Lord Winchilsea's, who was gone to the metropolis or we should have waited on his Lordship.

Thursday 30th December . From Oakham we breakfasted with Mr North, from whom Culley Harrison had gone on Monday for home. Mr North tells me Mr Harrison is to be married to Mrs Warcop and to live near Lemon Lane on an estate of the late Mr Warcops. We got to Dishley last night, where I found Lisle Johnson had set of with the young horses on Monday last, but was grievously disappointed that there was no letter for me, but concluded you had wrote to London but when Mr Bakewell received his letters from Mr Honeyborn this morning behold
no letter for poor me . News in suspense is torturing' says Shake. I pray God send me good news. As I have had no letter I shall most likely leave this place in 2 or 3 days (if weather permit for a quantity of snow is fallen this morning), shall stop a couple of days at Mr Sails, and so to Mr Colling where I hope to meet with a letter. We wanted much to know Mr T. Bates is, among other things. Last Monday market London was exceeding good for cattle and pretty good for sheep, previous to that very bad. Corn markets much same every where, but now expected to advance, at least not to fall lower. This weather has all the appearance of continuance but whether or not its always right to act with prudence. I should advise to use turnips and straw in every case you can, and save hay, because turnips are always to be feared in such severe frosty winters, but hay will keep and may be wanted, besides oats will advance in course I apprehend. I hope you have had a cheerful Christmas may you have a happy new year and many is the sincere wish of your much obliged and ever offed
Goo Culley
PS This family all join in compliments where due and wish to know of Mr Bates's health.
18. Dishley 1st January 1784
Dear Brother

How it has happened I know not but I have received no letters from you since that I received at Bury by the way of London of the 4th and 7th ult . You may believe I am anxious, but it is best to hope the best. I wrote to you from this place on Thursday, we arrived from our southern tour the day before, and this day I am determined to turn my face south north, as there seems no likelihood of a change. Monday 3rd January Doncaster. Mr Bakewell and I set out from Dishley on Saturday 1st and got to Nottingham market, and meeting with many acquaintances, amongst the rest Mr Deverel, Mr Bettison, Mr Breedon &c we spent the evening and staid all night at the White Lyon, where Mr Bakewell begun the new year (strange to tell) by letting Mr Breedon for 3 seasons to come the tupping of 40 ewes only, with any one tup Mr Bakewell has, Mr Breedon
to choose what tup, at 100 guineas each year, Mr Bakewell reserving the rest of the rode for his own use, or to dispose of, as he thinks best. This is making more than 200 guineas of one tup, what will they come to? Mr Breedon seemed happy at the offer made and was not long of making the bargain. At the same time Mr Bettison bid 120 guineas for the use of Cambrels, but Mr Bakewell would only let half his rode, and on the same terms as Mr Breedon had dealt. Mr Bettison and Deverel are to go to Dishley some day this week, and I do believe Mr Bettison (whatever Deverel may I know not) will do business, and I am clear Mr Bakewell will only let the half rodes of his best sheep at present, and of these for no less than 100 guineas for 40 ewes from one breeder only. For we had this talked over, and determined upon, on our way to Nottingham. It is very clear that he will do his sheep of character at strange prices. He says and I agree to it, that a customer will give no less but more for a tup, that you insist upon 20 or 30 ewes done by, it stamps a kind of value upon him, and a man will also give 100 for the tupping of 40 of his best ewes, by a capital tup, rather than hire one that is not tried at one third of the money. He considers all these matters over in every point of view, and then determines on a fixed price for the day, but alterable another day, if he sees right, but never the day he fixes the price. He says he finds much advantage, and trouble saved by these resolutions. I own that things never would have been so high, under any other administration as Mr Bakewells but he has now diffused such a spirit thorough this island, and the breeding is fixed upon such sound principles, that without we should lose our liberties or some other serious matter, this sort can never go out of fashion, nor this spirit subside. It snowed all the day yesterday as I came from Nottingham to this place, and wets a little this morning, but not a true thaw I think, the storm has upon the whole been a very mild one in the part of the country where we have been.

Wentbridge 3rd January 1785. I had some faint hopes of a letter at this place, but am again disappointed, what can be the matter that I have had no letter of so long a time, the old saying is that No News is good News' pray God send it good when I get it. I am determined to send you this today that you may still have time to write to me to Mr Collings at Shirningham which I shall make my head quarters, until I leave the county of Durham, pray Mr Matt if you have not leisure to write, get Dr Kerr to write how you all are. By a letter I had from Mr R. Colling, I am told Mr Wastle does not like Mr Thompsons little heifer, says she gets no weight, if they do not pay well, my friend Sail is as well without them. If I was not so anxious to hear how you all are this new year, I would go to
Wakefield market as it is on Wednesday however I fancy I shall still go because I would like to feel and see how things are going and like to go in this 2nd market in England, as much depends on that market to us and the north. Mr and Mrs Sail join in best wishes with your ever offed
Goo Culley
PS I never sent so short a letter before. Pray tell me how my friend Thomas Bates is, Lisle Johnson told them at Dishley that he was robbed as he went home, but I hope it was his brother he meant of.
19. Wentbridge 6th January 1785
Dear Brother

I sent you a letter from hence the other day, and did intend to have seen Wakefield market, but the weather was so wet we could not go. The snow all went here, and the waters much out, but a severe frost again this morning. I only wait N. Edisons arrival to tell us how the the market was, and then I steer north. Whitwell 7th January . Edison did not come so I turned for York, and at this place all night. I thought now I was here that I might as well see John Taylors tups, and Richard Barugh, and pay Richard for his pigs. An extreme frost, I begin to fear turnips, though there is no wind. William Walker of York says fat will be very scarce in this neighbourhood after a while, only the storm hastened many things to market, they sell best mutton and best prices beef at 4d per lb. Mr Sail sends his compliments to you and James.

Salton 7th January . I look upon this to be the happiest corner in this island, here is all the ancient English Christmas plenty and hospitality, all that rural festivity and honest simplicity of manners that characterizes a people above want yet untutored in the vices of the age. I let my friend John Taylor and his brother in law Hay the best sheep for next season again at same price 15 guineas. They paid me for last season, but John Taylor has not settled for the other, but will pay me at next meeting and if he cannot let him to somebody at 5 guineas more, will keep him again at 4 guineas. He says we shall have more customers from Milton side next year, and I hope we shall. I breakfasted this morning (Saturday 8th January ) at master Kendals, who said nothing, then I called on Mr Cleaver, who says he will have one of our best tups next season. Mr Cleaver is rather precipitate, therefore I will not be sure of this coming, however I may say as Mr Bakewell used to say of Lincolnshire 'these people must either come to me or somebody else'. This day a little more snow fell. I am now got to my old friend Mr Boroughs, but he is gone to Easingwold.
However I stay all night, and it suits very well, for I have both breeches and boots to mend, and no wonder, I believe want of clothes will drive me home if nothing else will. Whitby butchers have been buying beasts for the shipping, give 30s per cwt, Messrs Cleaver and Kendal &c say that fat will be scarce.

Sunday 9th January . Arrived at Mr Collings, where I saw a letter from James Culley acquainting Mr Colling that Morpeth market was only indifferent &c &c. (Monday 10th January ) I came to Darlington where I met with a letter from you, which had been at Dishley and which acquainted me of a letter sent by you to Mr Bells at London that I had no chance to receive. But I am glad to hear that my friend T. Bates is arrived safe. I am glad that you have sold so many ewes &c and that you have bought Lowry Gibsons turnips, it is certainly right rather than be fast, James poor fellow has all the trouble, but I hope to be with you soon to partake of the trouble, indeed its more than time. I propose if all be well to be at Morpeth on Tuesday come a week at the Phoenix where I shall be glad to see James &c. It will be Tuesday the 18th inst in the evening before the market. I sincerely wish my sister and Mrs Forty a happy time both. I think the two Jameses sold their sheep very well at Morpeth. I wish Sir Francis Blake &c good luck. I dined and Bob Colling with me at Mr Hills, and paid him for his bull calf I bespoke as I went south, it is a promising calf I think. I also bought and paid 9£ for a cow for a nurse for it. Mr Hill and Colling both think it best to send a single horse cart for it after a while, of that we must consider when I get home. I got to Denton this evening, and by Mr Peacocks advisement met M. Turner at John Woods where he made a tender of his rent provided I would allow him 3 interest for the times he has paid you his rent before due as he calls it saying he was only to pay his rent at Candlemass &c, but the truth is he wants to quarrel and does not know how. I told him I only acted as agent for you and that I had no right to allow interest without your leave, so he put up the money again. I shall speak to Mr Hardcastle about this matter before I leave this country. We had agreed, I mean Mr Peacock and I to send for Mr Dixon and get the article forwarded. I say article because on my calling on Mr Hardcastle this morning he told me an article would be sufficiently binding upon stamps. But as Mick Turner is so obstinate I know not what to do. However I think we will send for Mr Dixon and talk to him about this matter, as you are certainly bound to give Dixon legal possession of Denton farm at the term next ensuing. He Turner is certainly the most brutal animal living, he would gladly have quarrelled with Mr Peacock and me if we would
have differed with him. It is past 11 o'clock at night and I am sleepy, and you may be sure we will act to the best of our knowledge. So God bless you all.
Goo Culley
PS Tell James I shall be at Morpeth on Tuesday the 18th at the Phoenix.
